items.title: Insecure CORS Configuration (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's source code, specifically the CORS/middleware configuration files. A running build of the application (local or a test environment) and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the configuration's runtime behavior matches what the code implies.
items.whatItIs: Reading the code directly shows the setting controlling which websites may make cross-origin requests is too permissive. It may automatically trust whatever site is asking. It may allow any site at all while also permitting credentials. Or it may check the requesting site's name loosely — testing whether it merely contains the right word — instead of matching an exact list of allowed sites.
items.rootCause: This setting was written to quickly satisfy an immediate need — letting one or more frontends talk to the API — using the simplest possible approach (trust anything, or match loosely) instead of maintaining an exact, specific list of the actual sites that should be trusted.
items.impact: A malicious web page loaded in a victim's browser can make authenticated requests to the API using that victim's existing session, then read the responses back. From there it can pull data out or perform state-changing actions the victim is authorised for. How severe this is turns on one detail: whether credentialed requests are permitted alongside the loose origin matching, because without credentials the attacker gets far less.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the CORS configuration/middleware in source (searching for `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, a CORS middleware package's configuration block, or a custom origin-matching function).
Read the origin-matching logic precisely: does it echo the request's Origin header unconditionally, use a wildcard, or apply a substring/suffix match rather than an exact-match allowlist.

Check whether `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is also configured alongside the permissive origin match, which is the combination that makes the misconfiguration exploitable for credentialed requests.

Build and run the application locally with the identified configuration, then confirm the runtime behavior matches the source by sending a request with an arbitrary `Origin` header and inspecting the response.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes CORS-misconfiguration testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Send a test request with an arbitrary `Origin` header and confirm the response reflects it back (or otherwise matches the permissive pattern identified in source).
Build a benign proof-of-concept HTML page issuing a credentialed cross-origin request to the application from a different test origin.
Load the proof-of-concept page in a browser session authenticated to the application (a test account) and confirm the cross-origin response is successfully read.
Document the exact source location of the misconfigured origin-matching logic and the confirmed runtime exploitability.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for CORS configuration and origin-matching logic
Confirm runtime origin reflection
Proof-of-concept cross-origin credentialed request page

variants: Origin matched via a substring/suffix check (e.g. `origin.endsWith('.target.com')`) bypassable by registering a lookalike subdomain, versus a full wildcard/unconditional-reflection pattern.
Permissive CORS present only on a specific subset of routes (added by a different developer at a different time) rather than applied uniformly across the whole API.
mitigation: Replace the permissive origin-matching logic with an explicit, exact-match allowlist of specific, legitimate origins maintained centrally in configuration.
Never combine a wildcard or reflected-origin policy with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
Add a static-analysis rule or code-review checklist item specifically flagging CORS-configuration changes for mandatory security review before merge.
Include an automated test asserting the CORS policy's exact-match behavior (rejecting an unlisted test origin) in the CI test suite.

links: CWE-346 (Origin Validation Error)
OWASP WSTG-CLNT-07 (Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing)

items.title: Insecure Trust of Client-Supplied Content-Type Header in Code
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's file-upload-handling source code. A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to test the identified logic's runtime behavior.
items.whatItIs: Looking at the upload code directly: it decides what kind of file was uploaded — and how to handle it — based purely on what the client claims the file type is (through a header or the filename's extension), instead of actually inspecting the file's real content. An attacker can label a malicious file with an innocent-looking type and have it accepted.
items.rootCause: The claimed file type and filename extension are both values the client fully controls and can set to anything. Trusting either one for a security decision — like whether it's safe to store somewhere web-accessible — mixes up 'what the client says this is' with 'what it actually is,' and an attacker can easily make those two things different.
items.impact: An attacker uploads a file whose real content is dangerous — a web shell, or HTML carrying a script — while its declared type and extension claim it is something harmless like an image. Two outcomes follow. If the file is later served back with the attacker's declared type, it becomes stored cross-site scripting. If it lands somewhere the web server will execute, it becomes direct code execution.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the file-upload handling code and trace exactly what determines the file's accepted/rejected status and its stored/served type — the client-supplied `Content-Type` header, the filename's extension, or an independent content inspection.
Confirm whether any magic-byte/signature-based content verification exists at all, distinct from a client-supplied metadata check.

Build and run the application, then attempt to upload a file with mismatched content and declared type (e.g. an HTML file with a script payload, declared as `image/png` with a `.png` extension) and observe whether it's accepted.

If accepted, determine how the file is later served — with its stored, attacker-controlled Content-Type header, which would enable a browser to render/execute it as originally intended by the attacker despite the misleading extension.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes file-upload testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Craft a file whose actual content is an XSS payload (or a web-shell script for a server-side-execution scenario) with a mismatched, innocuous-looking declared Content-Type/extension.
Upload the crafted file and confirm it's accepted despite the content/type mismatch.

Access the uploaded file via its resulting URL and confirm whether it's served in a way that triggers the embedded payload (executed as script, or served with a Content-Type causing the browser to render rather than download it).
Document the exact source location of the trust-in-client-supplied-type logic and the confirmed runtime exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for Content-Type-based file-type determination
Upload a mismatched-content file declared as an image
Access the uploaded file to check served Content-Type/execution

variants: Trust in the client-supplied filename extension alone (no Content-Type check at all) versus trust in the Content-Type header specifically — both share the same underlying flaw of trusting client-controlled metadata.
Mismatch exploited for stored XSS (the file is later rendered in a browser context) versus for direct server-side code execution (the file lands in a web-servable, script-executing directory).
mitigation: Independently verify uploaded file content against its claimed type using magic-byte/signature inspection (or a dedicated file-type-detection library) rather than trusting the client-supplied Content-Type header or filename extension.

Store uploaded files outside the web root, or in a location configured to never execute scripts, serving them only through a controlled download/proxy endpoint that sets its own, verified Content-Type.
Apply an allowlist of permitted, verified file types for the specific upload feature, rejecting anything outside it regardless of what the client claims.
Set a restrictive Content-Security-Policy and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on any response serving user-uploaded content, as defense in depth against browser content-type sniffing.

links: CWE-646 (Reliance on File Name or Extension of Externally-Supplied File)
OWASP WSTG-BUSL-09 (Test Upload of Unexpected File Types)

items.title: Hardcoded Credentials
items.prerequisites: Read access to the full application source code and its version-control history (not just the current HEAD, since a credential may have been removed from the latest commit but remain in history). Standard string-search and secret-scanning tools (grep/ripgrep, gitleaks, truffleHog).
items.whatItIs: The source code has a password, API key, or other credential typed directly into it, or into a configuration file that's checked into the code repository — instead of being loaded securely at runtime from an environment variable or a proper secrets service.
items.rootCause: Typing a credential straight into the code is the fastest way to get something working during development. Without an automated scan checking for this during code review, it's easy to miss — especially when the credential was added quickly to unblock one specific task, rather than through a careful, reviewed setup process.
items.impact: Anyone who can read the repository gets the credential directly. That includes every developer, anyone holding a leaked copy, and the general public if the repository is or ever becomes public. Worse, because it is committed in code it also survives in every historical commit, fork, backup and mirror indefinitely. Removing it from the current version does not remove it.
stepsToIdentify: Run an automated secret-scanning tool across the full repository, including its complete commit history, not just the current working tree.

Manually grep for common credential-indicating patterns (`password =`, `api_key =`, `secret =`, cloud-provider key formats) as a complement to automated scanning, which can miss non-standard variable naming.
For each candidate found, trace its usage to confirm it's a genuine, live credential rather than an obviously-fake placeholder/example value.

Where a credential was found removed from the current HEAD but present in history, confirm whether it was also rotated, since removal from the current commit alone doesn't invalidate a credential that remains readable in history.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes credential extraction and, where applicable, validation from the reviewed source code/repository.
Run secret-scanning across the full repository history and manually review flagged candidates.
For each confirmed candidate, validate its live status and scope of access using a minimal, read-only check appropriate to the credential type.
Document every discovered credential, its exact source location (including whether it's only in history versus also the current HEAD), and its validated scope of access.
Recommend immediate rotation for any confirmed live, exposed credential as an urgent finding, independent of the rest of the report.

examplePayloads.label: Scan the full repository history for hardcoded credentials
Manually grep for common credential patterns
Validate a discovered database credential (read-only check)

variants: Credential present in the current HEAD (immediately, actively exposed to anyone with repo access) versus only in historical commits (still exposed to anyone who clones the full history, but easy to overlook if only the current tree is reviewed).
A single, shared credential used across every environment (dev/staging/production all using the same hardcoded value), multiplying the impact of a single exposure.
mitigation: Remove all hardcoded credentials from source code, supplying them at runtime via environment variables or a dedicated secrets-management service instead.
Add automated secret-scanning as a mandatory pre-commit hook and CI pipeline gate, blocking any commit/merge introducing a detected credential pattern.
Rotate any credential confirmed to have ever been committed to the repository, since simply removing it from the current commit doesn't invalidate a value still readable in history.

Where history itself needs remediation (a credential is too sensitive to leave in history indefinitely), consider a history-rewriting/purge process in addition to rotation, understanding the operational disruption this causes for a shared repository.

links: CWE-321 (Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key)
OWASP WSTG-CONF-04 (Review Old Backup and Unreferenced Files for Sensitive Information)

items.title: Insufficient Entropy in Session Token Generation (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the source code responsible for generating session tokens/identifiers. A running build of the application to collect a sample of generated tokens for statistical validation of the source-level finding.
items.whatItIs: Looking directly at the code that generates session tokens: it uses a source of randomness that isn't actually unpredictable enough for something this sensitive — an ordinary random function instead of a cryptographically secure one, or a token built mostly from predictable pieces like a timestamp or a simple counter.
items.rootCause: A session token needs to be just as unpredictable as an encryption key. But reaching for a standard, everyday random function (which is simpler, and fine for non-security uses) instead of deliberately choosing a cryptographically secure one is an easy mistake to make, especially if it's not obvious from the surrounding code that this particular value is actually security-critical.
items.impact: An attacker who works out the generator's pattern and its starting value can predict other users' session tokens. For well-documented non-secure random functions this is straightforward, since the internal state can often be rebuilt from a handful of observed outputs. They then hijack sessions directly, without needing to steal a token through cross-site scripting or network interception first.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the exact code path generating session tokens/identifiers and identify the specific randomness API used.

Confirm whether the API is a cryptographically secure generator (`SecureRandom`, `crypto.randomBytes`) or a standard, non-cryptographic one (`Math.random()`, `java.util.Random`, a weak hash of predictable input).
Where a CSPRNG is used, check how it's seeded, since a predictable seed can undermine an otherwise-correct algorithm choice.

Collect a sample of generated tokens from a running build (for test accounts) and statistically analyze them for patterns consistent with the weak generator identified in source, confirming the source-level finding is practically exploitable.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes token-sample collection and predictability analysis against a running build of the reviewed application.
Extract or replicate the exact generation algorithm and seeding logic identified in source.
Collect a representative sample of generated session tokens for test accounts.
Attempt to reconstruct the generator's internal state from the collected sample and predict a subsequent token value.
Confirm the predicted token is accepted as a valid session identifier by the application, demonstrating practical session-hijacking feasibility.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for session-token generation and its randomness source
Collect a sample of generated tokens for statistical analysis
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s -c - https://app.target.com/login -d 'user=test'$i'&pass=testpass' | grep -i sessionid; done

examplePayloads.label: Statistically test collected tokens for predictability

variants: Non-cryptographic PRNG used directly for the token versus a cryptographically-appropriate generator undermined by a predictable seed (timestamp-based).
Weak randomness affecting session tokens specifically versus other security-critical identifiers generated by the same weak routine (password-reset tokens, API keys) elsewhere in the codebase.
mitigation: Use a cryptographically secure random number generator for every session token/identifier and any other security-critical random value.
Never seed a CSPRNG with a predictable value; rely on the platform's own properly-sourced entropy for seeding.
Audit the codebase for every randomness-generation call site as part of a security-focused code review, distinguishing security-sensitive uses from genuinely non-sensitive ones.
Ensure session tokens carry sufficient length/entropy (128 bits or more of true randomness) regardless of the specific generator chosen.

links: CWE-330 (Use of Insufficiently Random Values)
OWASP WSTG-SESS-01 (Testing for Session Management Schema)

items.title: Server-Side Authentication Bypass Logic
items.prerequisites: Read access to the authentication-logic source code. A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the identified logic flaw's runtime behavior.
items.whatItIs: Reading the actual login-checking code reveals a specific coding mistake that lets someone in without a valid password. It might be an 'if' condition written backwards or with a subtle bug. It might be code returning success before the password check has finished running. It might be a comparison that a specially crafted input can trick. Or a 'remember me' or single-sign-on path that skips the real password check entirely under certain conditions.
items.rootCause: Login logic tends to accumulate multiple paths over time — regular password login, single sign-on, 'remember me,' API-key login — often added by different developers at different times. A subtle bug in any one of those paths can create a bypass. This is fundamentally a coding mistake in security-critical logic, and it's the kind of thing that's often only really catchable by carefully reading the exact code, not just testing the app from outside.
items.impact: An attacker who finds and triggers the flawed condition achieves a complete authentication bypass, logging in as any user including an administrator, with no valid credential at all. This ranks among the most severe findings possible. Every other control in the application is built on the assumption that authentication is a reliable gate, and that assumption no longer holds.
stepsToIdentify: Read the complete authentication-logic code path line by line, tracing every conditional branch from request receipt to the final authenticated/rejected decision, for every supported authentication method (password, SSO, remember-me, API key).

Pay particular attention to negation operators, early-return statements, and comparison operators (especially loose/coercive equality in dynamically-typed languages) that could behave unexpectedly for a specific, crafted input.
For each suspicious construct identified, reason through what specific input would trigger the unintended code path, and note it as a hypothesis to validate at runtime.
Build and run the application, then attempt the crafted input against the identified code path to confirm whether the bypass is practically exploitable.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes authentication-bypass testing against a running build of the reviewed application, using the specific flaw identified via source review.
Craft the specific request/input identified as likely to trigger the flawed conditional logic.
Submit the crafted request and confirm whether authentication succeeds without a valid credential.
Where successful, confirm the resulting session grants access as the targeted (or an arbitrary) user account.
Document the exact source location and line(s) of the flawed logic, and the confirmed runtime bypass.

examplePayloads.label: Trace the full authentication logic path in source
Test a suspected type-coercion bypass in a loose-equality comparison
Test a suspected early-return/negation-logic bypass with a crafted parameter

variants: Bypass via a flawed password-comparison conditional versus via an SSO/remember-me code path that skips the primary check entirely under a specific, attacker-triggerable condition.
Bypass exploitable pre-authentication by any anonymous caller versus requiring some prior, lesser level of access to reach the flawed code path.
mitigation: Rewrite the flawed conditional logic with clear, explicit, positively-stated checks ("access is granted only if X is true") rather than negated or implicitly-inverted conditions that are easy to get subtly wrong.
Use strict equality/type-checking throughout authentication logic, never relying on a language's loose-equality or type-coercion behavior for a security-critical comparison.
Apply a fail-closed design principle throughout — any unexpected code path, exception, or unhandled condition during authentication should result in a rejected login, never an implicit success.

Include comprehensive unit and integration tests covering every authentication code path and edge case (empty/null credentials, malformed input, every supported auth method) as a standing regression suite.

links: CWE-697 (Incorrect Comparison)
OWASP WSTG-ATHN-04 (Testing for Bypassing Authentication Schema)

items.title: Improper Session Management (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the session-management source code (session creation, regeneration, and invalidation logic). A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) capable of manipulating and reusing session identifiers across requests.
items.whatItIs: The session-handling code fails to issue a brand-new session ID at a key moment — most commonly, right after someone successfully logs in. That means a session ID that existed before login (one an attacker might have set up in advance and tricked the victim into using, or simply observed) keeps working as the actual authenticated session once login completes.
items.rootCause: Preventing this kind of attack requires a deliberate step — explicitly generating a fresh session ID at the exact moment someone's access level changes, especially at login. That step is easy to miss if the session framework being used doesn't do it automatically, or if the session-handling code was custom-built without this specific protection in mind.
items.impact: An attacker first gets the victim to use a session identifier they already know. They might do that through a URL parameter that accepts a session ID, a predictable cookie-setting mechanism, or simply by setting the cookie on a shared or kiosk machine before the victim arrives. Once the victim logs in, that same identifier is now authenticated, and the attacker uses it themselves. No credential and no post-login token ever needs to be stolen.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the session-creation and login-handling code and trace whether a new session identifier is generated/issued specifically at the point of successful authentication, versus the pre-login session identifier simply being "upgraded" to an authenticated state in place.
Build and run the application, then capture the session identifier issued before login.

Complete a login using that same pre-established session identifier (not allowing the client to accept a new cookie if one is offered) and confirm whether the identifier remains valid and now represents the authenticated session.
Where regeneration is confirmed absent, also check for the same gap at other privilege-transition points (a password change, an MFA step-up) beyond just the initial login.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes session-fixation testing against a running build of the reviewed application, using a nominated test account.
Capture a session identifier from an unauthenticated request (before any login).
Set that same session identifier deliberately on a second client/session and complete the login flow for the test account using it.
Confirm whether the pre-established session identifier remains valid post-login and now grants authenticated access, using a separate request that presents only that original identifier.
Document the exact source location where regeneration is missing and the confirmed runtime session-fixation exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Trace login handling for session-ID regeneration
Capture a pre-login session identifier
Complete login while retaining the pre-established session cookie, then confirm it remains valid
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -X POST https://app.target.com/login -d 'user=testaccount&pass=testpass'
curl -s -b cookies.txt https://app.target.com/account  # confirm authenticated access using the original, pre-login session ID

variants: Missing regeneration at login specifically versus at other privilege-transition points (password change, MFA completion, privilege elevation) — each represents a distinct instance of the same underlying gap.
Session-fixation exploitable via a URL-parameter-accepted session ID (the most severe, trivially attacker-supplied variant) versus only via a shared/kiosk-browser pre-set-cookie scenario.
mitigation: Regenerate the session identifier explicitly at every privilege-transition point — most critically immediately upon successful login — invalidating the pre-existing, pre-authentication session identifier entirely.
Never accept a session identifier via a URL parameter; use cookies exclusively (with appropriate Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite attributes) for session-identifier transport.
Use a well-maintained, security-reviewed session-management framework/library that handles regeneration automatically by default, rather than a custom implementation, wherever feasible.
Include an automated test asserting the session identifier changes across the login transition in the standard regression-test suite.

links: OWASP WSTG-SESS-03 (Testing for Session Fixation)

items.title: Improper Privilege Management in Code
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's role/privilege-management source code. A running build of the application and valid credentials for at least two accounts of different intended privilege levels to confirm the identified logic gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The code that assigns, checks or upgrades a user's permission level has a flaw letting someone end up with more access than intended. That might be a function defaulting to admin-level access when an expected value is missing. It might be an admin-promotion feature with no check on who may call it. Or a role read from something the client controls, such as a cookie or token, instead of being confirmed independently on the server every time.
items.rootCause: This kind of code is usually written and tested for the normal, expected case. Too little thought goes into what happens when something unexpected or missing shows up — such as defaulting to a high-privilege role rather than the lowest one when input is absent. The other half of the problem is whether the function that actually grants elevated access has its own permission check guarding who may call it.
items.impact: A user ends up with more privilege than intended, or can grant it to themselves or another account. How far that goes depends on the specific flaw. It might be a minor expansion of which features they can reach, or it might be complete administrative control of the application.
stepsToIdentify: Locate all code responsible for assigning or checking user roles/privileges, including account-creation defaults, role-elevation/promotion functions, and any place a role value is read from a client-supplied source (a JWT claim, a cookie, a hidden form field).

For a role-assignment default, trace what happens if the expected input determining the role is missing/null — does the code default to the least-privileged role, or does an unhandled case inadvertently resolve to something more permissive.
For a role-elevation/promotion function, confirm it has its own, independent authorization check restricting who can invoke it, separate from simply being an authenticated user.

For any role value sourced from client-modifiable data, confirm whether the server treats it as authoritative without re-deriving/re-validating it against the actual, stored account role on each request.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes privilege-management testing against a running build of the reviewed application, using the provided test accounts.

Using the identified logic gap, attempt to trigger the unintended-elevation path — omitting the expected role-determining input at account creation, invoking the promotion function without the expected authorization, or modifying a client-supplied role claim/cookie value.
Confirm whether the resulting account/session ends up with elevated privilege beyond what was legitimately intended.
Demonstrate the practical impact by accessing functionality that should require the higher privilege level.
Document the exact source location of the privilege-management flaw and the confirmed runtime escalation achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Trace role-assignment logic for an unhandled/default-elevated case
Attempt account creation with the role-determining input omitted
Attempt to modify a client-supplied role claim and confirm server-side re-validation (or its absence)

variants: Unintended-elevation-by-default in an account-creation code path versus an unguarded privilege-elevation/promotion function callable by any authenticated user.
Client-supplied role value trusted without server-side re-validation, allowing direct client-side privilege claim forgery, distinct from a logic-flaw-driven unintended default.
mitigation: Default every role-assignment code path to the least-privileged role explicitly, treating any missing/unexpected input as a reason to assign minimal privilege, never an elevated one.
Apply an explicit, independent authorization check to every privilege-elevation/promotion function, verifying the caller genuinely holds the authority to grant the requested privilege change.
Never trust a client-supplied value (a JWT claim, a cookie) as the authoritative source of a user's current role; re-derive and verify it server-side from the stored account record on every request.
Include privilege-management-specific test cases (missing inputs, unauthorized promotion attempts, forged role claims) in the standard security-focused test suite.

links: CWE-250 (Execution with Unnecessary Privileges)
OWASP WSTG-ATHZ-02 (Testing for Bypassing Authorization Schema)

items.title: Missing/Improper Authorization Check
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's request-handling/controller source code for a representative set of endpoints. A running build of the application and valid credentials for at least two accounts of differing privilege/ownership to confirm the identified gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: A specific piece of code handling a sensitive action — returning data, changing a record, doing something admin-level — correctly checks that the caller is logged in, but never actually checks whether they're allowed to do this specific thing. Tracing through the code directly confirms there's no ownership or role check anywhere in that path at all.
items.rootCause: A permission check has to be deliberately added to every sensitive piece of code — it doesn't happen automatically. It's easy for one specific endpoint (especially one added later, or copied from a similar one without adjusting the checks, or one whose sensitivity the original developer didn't fully appreciate) to simply never get that check written in the first place — as opposed to having a check that's just flawed.
items.impact: Any authenticated caller — or in the worst cases an unauthenticated one — can invoke the affected function and perform whatever it does, with no ownership or role requirement standing in the way. This is the complete absence of a control rather than a weak one, so severity tracks directly with how sensitive the unprotected function happens to be.
stepsToIdentify: For each endpoint/function handling a sensitive action, trace its complete execution path from request receipt to the action being performed, explicitly confirming whether an authorization check (ownership verification, role check) exists anywhere in that path.

Pay particular attention to newer endpoints, endpoints that appear structurally similar to another, properly-authorized endpoint (suggesting a copy-paste origin that may have dropped the check), and endpoints reached via an unusual or secondary code path (a batch-operation handler, an internal API called by another service).
For any function found with no authorization check at all, confirm this isn't compensated for by a check performed earlier in a shared middleware chain that the specific route might bypass.
Build and run the application, then confirm the finding at runtime by invoking the function using an account that should not be authorized for it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes missing-authorization-check testing against a running build of the reviewed application, using the provided test accounts.
Identify the specific function confirmed via source review to lack any authorization check.
Invoke it using an account/token that should not be permitted to perform the action (a different user's context, or a lower-privilege role).
Confirm the action succeeds despite the caller's lack of legitimate authorization.
Document the exact source location of the missing check and the confirmed runtime impact.

examplePayloads.label: Trace an endpoint handler's complete execution path for an authorization check
Invoke the identified unprotected function using an unauthorized test account

variants: Missing check on a REST endpoint versus on a GraphQL mutation/resolver, the latter being easier to overlook given GraphQL's single-endpoint model spreading authorization logic across many individual resolvers.
Missing check reachable directly via the primary API versus only reachable via a secondary, internal-facing batch/bulk-operation endpoint that processes the same underlying action differently.
mitigation: Apply a consistent, centrally-enforced authorization-check pattern (a decorator, middleware, or a mandatory code-review checklist item) to every function performing a sensitive action, rather than implementing checks ad hoc per endpoint.

Adopt a default-deny design principle — require an explicit, positive authorization grant for every sensitive action, rather than defaulting to allow and only adding restrictions where a gap is later noticed.
Include an automated test suite systematically verifying every endpoint/function enforces the expected authorization requirement, run as part of routine CI, not just periodic external assessments.
Apply particular scrutiny during code review to newly-added or copy-paste-derived endpoints specifically for this class of omission.

links: CWE-285 (Improper Authorization)
OWASP WSTG-ATHZ-02 (Testing for Bypassing Authorization Schema)

items.title: Time-of-Check Authorization Drift
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code implementing a multi-step operation where an authorization check and the actual privileged action are separated in time (a check-then-act pattern). A running build of the application and the ability to manipulate timing/state (a second client session, or a race-condition tool) to test the identified gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The code correctly checks that someone is allowed to do something at one point in time — but then a meaningful gap (time, or a separate processing step) happens before the actual sensitive action runs. During that gap, the person's permission could change — their role could get revoked, ownership of the resource could shift — but the code never re-checks; it just trusts the earlier result even though it might no longer be true.
items.rootCause: Splitting a permission check from the actual action it's checking for is a pretty natural result of multi-step processes — an approval flow, a background job queue, a multi-step form. But if the code doesn't re-check permission right when the action actually happens, there's a window where the earlier check has gone stale compared to what's actually true right now.
items.impact: An attacker whose permission is revoked during the gap between the check and the action still gets that action performed, using permission they no longer hold. A privileged action queued before an account was downgraded still completes. So does one queued before access to a specific resource was withdrawn. The revocation appears to have worked while the old decision is still being acted on.
stepsToIdentify: Identify multi-step or asynchronous processing flows where an authorization check occurs at one point (e.g. when a request is submitted/queued) and the actual privileged action occurs at a later, separate point (e.g. when a background job processes the queued request).
Trace whether the later action re-verifies the caller's current authorization state immediately before executing, or simply trusts that the earlier check's result remains valid.
Where source access allows, identify a specific scenario to test: revoking a permission/role between the initial check and the action's eventual execution.

Build and run the application, then reproduce the timing scenario (submit the action, then revoke the relevant permission before the queued/delayed action actually executes) to confirm the gap at runtime.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes time-of-check/time-of-use authorization-drift testing against a running build of the reviewed application, using a nominated test account whose permissions can be safely modified during the test.
Initiate the multi-step action using the test account while it holds the required permission, ensuring the action's actual execution is delayed (queued, async-processed) as identified in source.
Before the action actually executes, revoke the test account's relevant permission/role.
Confirm whether the delayed action still executes successfully despite the account no longer holding the required permission at execution time.
Document the exact source location of the missing re-verification step and the confirmed runtime authorization-drift exploitation.

Submit a privileged action while holding permission, then revoke it before execution completes

curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/reports/schedule -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"reportType":"financial","delay":"60s"}'
# then, with admin test access, revoke the test account's report-generation permission before the 60s delay elapses

examplePayloads.label: Confirm whether the delayed action executed despite the revoked permission

variants: Authorization drift in an async job-queue processing flow versus in a multi-step, multi-request UI wizard where the final submission step doesn't re-check permission established in an earlier step.
Drift affecting a single user's own changing permission level versus affecting a resource's ownership transfer (the action executes against a resource the caller no longer owns by the time it runs).
mitigation: Re-verify authorization immediately before executing any privileged action, regardless of how much time has elapsed since an earlier check, rather than trusting a stale, earlier authorization result.
Where feasible, minimize the time window between check and action by combining them into a single, atomic operation.

For genuinely unavoidable async/queued processing, design the queue-processing worker to independently re-check authorization against the current, live permission state at the moment it dequeues and executes the action.
Include a specific test case simulating a permission revocation during the check-to-action window in the security-focused regression-test suite for any multi-step, permission-gated flow.

links: CWE-367 (Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition)

items.title: Command Injection (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's source code, specifically any location invoking an OS shell command or process (exec/system/subprocess-style calls). A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the identified injection point at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The application builds a system command — to run a utility, convert a file, or check the network — by pasting caller-supplied input directly into the command text, instead of passing values through a safe method that doesn't interpret them as shell instructions. An attacker can slip in extra command syntax that the operating system runs alongside, or instead of, the intended command.
items.rootCause: Running a command through a function that interprets it as if typed into a shell, and building the text of that command by simple concatenation, treats caller-supplied input as if it were safe, pre-written command syntax instead of untrusted data. Any special shell characters in that input then get interpreted as commands, not as plain text.
items.impact: This is full arbitrary command execution on the server, running with whatever privileges the application process holds. It sits among the most severe findings possible, because it leads directly to complete server compromise, movement into other internal systems, and access to any data or credentials that server can reach.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for every call site invoking an OS command via a shell-interpreting function, and trace each one back to confirm whether any part of the constructed command string originates from caller-supplied input.
For each candidate, confirm whether the caller-supplied portion is passed as a properly-separated argument (safe) or concatenated directly into a single command string (vulnerable).
Build and run the application, then submit a test input containing a shell metacharacter (a semicolon followed by a benign, verifiable command like `id` or `whoami`) to the identified parameter.

Confirm whether the injected command executes by observing its output reflected in the response, or an out-of-band side effect (a DNS/HTTP callback to a controlled listener) if the response doesn't directly reflect command output.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes command-injection testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Submit a test payload appending a benign, verifiable command via a shell metacharacter to the identified vulnerable parameter.
Confirm command execution via reflected output or an out-of-band callback.
Where confirmed, demonstrate impact with a further benign, non-destructive command (reading a non-sensitive system file, or confirming outbound network capability) rather than any destructive action.
Document the exact source location of the vulnerable command construction and the confirmed runtime code execution.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for shell-interpreting command execution with concatenated input
Test command injection via a shell metacharacter appended to the vulnerable parameter
Out-of-band confirmation if response doesn't reflect output

variants: Direct command injection via shell metacharacters versus argument injection (the input is passed as a single argument without shell interpretation, but its value can still manipulate the invoked command's own flags/behavior in an unintended way).
Injection reachable pre-authentication on a public-facing endpoint versus only reachable by an authenticated user, affecting real-world severity/exploitability.
mitigation: Avoid invoking OS commands via a shell-interpreting function entirely wherever possible; use a language-native library/API to perform the equivalent task directly (a file-manipulation library instead of shelling out to a CLI tool).

Where invoking an external command is unavoidable, use an API that passes arguments as a separate, non-shell-interpreted array/list (e.g. `subprocess.run([...], shell=False)`) rather than a single, concatenated command string.
Apply strict allowlist input validation on any value that must be incorporated into a command, rejecting anything containing shell metacharacters outright.
Run the process invoking external commands with the minimum OS-level privileges necessary, limiting the impact of any injection that does occur despite other mitigations.

links: CWE-77 (Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command)
OWASP WSTG-INPV-12 (Testing for Command Injection)

items.title: Insecure Deserialization (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code invoking a deserialization function (native serialization APIs, or a library like Java's ObjectInputStream, .NET's BinaryFormatter, Python's pickle). A gadget-chain generation tool (ysoserial/ysoserial.net) and a running build of the application to confirm the identified issue at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The application loads data from a source that could plausibly be attacker-controlled — a cookie, an uploaded file, a message from an internal queue — using a format (like .NET's BinaryFormatter, Java's native serialization, or Python's pickle) that can reconstruct any kind of object the data describes, not just simple, safe data. If an attacker can tamper with that data, they can build a malicious object that runs their own code the moment it gets loaded.
items.rootCause: These formats work by directly building whatever object type the data says to build and running its setup code along the way, with no built-in restriction on what types are allowed. If the app has other, unrelated classes that can be chained together in unexpected ways, that chain can be used to run arbitrary code. Reading the code directly, this is confirmed by finding where the app loads this kind of data and tracing that input back to something an attacker can actually control.
items.impact: An attacker who can supply or tamper with the serialised data achieves arbitrary code execution inside the process doing the loading. This is among the most severe findings possible, since the path to full application and server compromise is direct rather than requiring further steps.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for calls to type-permissive native deserialization functions (`ObjectInputStream.readObject`, `BinaryFormatter.Deserialize`, `pickle.loads`, `yaml.load` without a safe loader).
For each call site, trace the data source back to confirm whether it originates from anything attacker-influenceable — a cookie, a file upload, a message queue an external party can write to.

Where a plausible attacker-reachable deserialization call is found, identify the exact serializer/library and version in use, since gadget-chain availability depends on which classes/libraries are loaded by the application.
Confirm whether any type-allowlisting (a custom `ObjectInputFilter`/`SerializationBinder`) is applied restricting deserialization to expected types.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes deserialization-based code-execution testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Generate a malicious serialized payload using a public gadget-chain tool targeting a chain compatible with the application's identified loaded libraries.
Deliver the payload via the confirmed attacker-reachable data path (a cookie value, an uploaded file, a queue message) and trigger deserialization.
Confirm code execution via a benign proof-of-concept command (writing a test file, a network callback to a controlled listener).
Document the exact source location of the vulnerable deserialization call, the gadget chain used, and the confirmed runtime code execution.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for type-permissive deserialization calls
Generate a gadget-chain payload for a Java target
Deliver the payload via an identified attacker-reachable cookie value

variants: Deserialization triggered via a cookie/session-token value versus via an uploaded file or an internal message-queue payload — the attacker-reachability and authentication precondition differ by data path.
Partial mitigation present (a type allowlist) that's itself bypassable due to an overly broad type-name pattern, versus no allowlist at all.
mitigation: Replace type-permissive native serializers with a safe, schema-constrained format (JSON with strict schema validation, protobuf) wherever the application controls both ends of the serialization.
Where native serialization cannot be avoided, implement a strict type-allowlist permitting only the specific, minimal set of types the application genuinely needs to deserialize.
Never deserialize data from an untrusted or externally-writable source without independent integrity verification (a signature over the serialized bytes, checked before deserialization begins).
Keep the application's dependency set minimal and current, since gadget-chain availability depends heavily on which library versions are loaded.

reference.standard: A08:2021 - Software and Data Integrity Failures
links: CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code)
OWASP WSTG-INPV-16 (Testing for Deserialization)

items.title: SQL Injection (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's data-access-layer source code (raw query-construction functions or ORM usage). A running build of the application and sqlmap for automated confirmation/exploitation of any identified injection point.
items.whatItIs: The application builds a database query by pasting caller-supplied input directly into the query text, instead of using the standard safe method (parameterized queries) that keeps user input clearly separated from the query's actual logic. This is confirmed directly in the code by finding the exact spot where a value from a request gets inserted into a query using string concatenation instead of being passed in safely.
items.rootCause: Pasting values directly into a query is the most obvious way to build a dynamic one. Even though safe, parameterized queries are well-known best practice, a specific spot in the code — especially a 'raw query' shortcut in a codebase that otherwise handles this safely — can still get written unsafely, particularly under time pressure or by someone less familiar with how the rest of the codebase normally does it.
items.impact: An attacker extracts arbitrary data from the database, bypassing every access control the application enforces above it. Depending on the exact syntax context and the database account's privileges, it can go further: modifying data, defeating authentication logic, or on some database engines reaching operating system level through the engine's own extended functionality.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for raw SQL query construction — string concatenation or formatting used to build a query string, particularly any raw-query escape hatch used alongside an otherwise ORM-based codebase.
For each candidate, trace the concatenated variable back to confirm it originates from caller-supplied input (a request parameter, a header, a cookie value) rather than a fixed, internal constant.

Build and run the application, then submit a syntax-breaking test value (a single quote) to the identified parameter and observe whether the response indicates a database error or unhandled exception.
Where a syntax-breaking response is confirmed, use sqlmap to formally confirm and characterize the injection.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes injection testing against a running build of the reviewed application, for the specific parameter identified via source review.
Send a syntax-breaking test value and confirm an anomalous response indicating unsanitized query construction.
Run sqlmap against the identified parameter to confirm and characterize the injection technique applicable to the specific database engine in use.
Extract a minimal, non-destructive proof-of-concept data sample (the database version string, a single test-account record) rather than a bulk data dump.
Document the exact source location of the vulnerable query-construction code and the confirmed runtime exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for raw, concatenated SQL query construction
Test for a syntax-breaking response
Automated confirmation and exploitation with sqlmap

variants: Injection in a raw-query escape hatch within an otherwise ORM-based codebase (an easier gap to overlook precisely because most of the codebase is otherwise safe by convention) versus a codebase built without an ORM at all, where every query is individually at risk.

First-order injection (the malicious input is used immediately in a query) versus second-order (the input is stored via one code path and only triggers injection when a separate, later query incorporates the stored value unsafely).
mitigation: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements (or the ORM's safe query-building methods) for every query incorporating caller-supplied input, eliminating raw-query string concatenation entirely.

Where a raw-query escape hatch is genuinely necessary for a case the ORM doesn't support, apply the same parameterization discipline within that raw query rather than falling back to string concatenation.
Apply the principle of least privilege to the database account the application uses, limiting the blast radius of any injection that does occur.
Add a static-analysis (SAST) rule flagging raw string concatenation into a query-construction call as a mandatory code-review blocker.

links: OWASP WSTG-INPV-05 (Testing for SQL Injection)

items.title: Server-Side Template Injection (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code that renders a template using a caller-influenceable value as part of the template string itself (rather than as data passed into a fixed template). A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the identified injection point at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The application builds a page template dynamically by mixing caller-supplied input directly into the template's own logic and syntax (instead of only ever using that input as plain data plugged into a fixed, pre-written template), then hands the combined result to a template engine to process. That lets an attacker inject template syntax the engine will actually interpret and run — which, for many popular template engines, can extend all the way to running arbitrary code.
items.rootCause: Template engines are specifically designed to execute logic — loops, conditionals, function calls — written inside a template. That's completely safe as long as the template's structure itself is fixed, developer-written code, and only the data plugged into it comes from users. But if user input gets mixed into the template's structure before it's processed, the attacker's input gets treated as logic to execute, not as harmless data.
items.impact: How far this goes depends on the template engine and whether it sandboxes anything, and many do not by default. At the lower end it behaves like content injection, similar to cross-site scripting. At the upper end it is full server-side code execution. For engines that expose the underlying language's objects and functions without restriction, this is frequently a direct route to complete application and server compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for template-rendering calls where the template string itself (not just the data context passed into it) is built via concatenation or formatting incorporating caller-supplied input.

Identify the specific template engine in use, since exploitation payloads and the achievable impact ceiling differ significantly between engines (Jinja2/Python, Twig/PHP, FreeMarker/Java, Handlebars/JavaScript).

Build and run the application, then submit a template-engine-specific probe expression (e.g. `{{7*7}}` for Jinja2/Twig) to the identified input and observe whether the response reflects the evaluated result (`49`) rather than the literal probe string, confirming the input reaches template compilation.
Where confirmed, escalate to an engine-specific payload targeting known code-execution gadgets/objects reachable from that engine's expression language.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SSTI testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Submit the template-engine-specific arithmetic probe to the identified input and confirm evaluated-result reflection.
Escalate to a known code-execution payload for the confirmed engine, targeting a benign, verifiable proof-of-concept action (reading a non-sensitive file, or an out-of-band callback).
Confirm the payload executes as proof of full server-side code execution.
Document the exact source location of the vulnerable template-string construction, the confirmed engine, and the demonstrated code-execution impact.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for caller input concatenated into a template string before rendering
Jinja2/Twig arithmetic probe to confirm template compilation
Jinja2 code-execution payload (Python-based engine)

variants: SSTI in a Python-based engine (Jinja2) with a well-documented, powerful sandbox-escape chain to full code execution, versus an engine with a more restrictive default sandbox (some FreeMarker/Twig configurations) where impact may be limited to content injection rather than full RCE.
SSTI triggered via a user-facing input field versus via an internal, less-obvious data path (an email-template-generation feature incorporating a user's display name unsanitized into the template).
mitigation: Never construct a template string dynamically by incorporating caller-supplied input into the template syntax itself; use a fixed, developer-authored template and pass all user input purely as data values within its rendering context.
If dynamic template selection is genuinely required, select from a strict, predefined allowlist of template files/names rather than building template content from user input.

Where the template engine offers a sandboxed rendering mode, enable and rigorously test it, understanding many "sandboxes" have documented escape techniques and shouldn't be relied upon as the sole protection.
Apply strict input validation to any value that must be used in a template-selection context, rejecting anything resembling template-engine syntax.

links: OWASP WSTG-INPV-18 (Testing for Server-Side Template Injection)

items.title: Business Logic Flaw in Discount Calculation Function
items.prerequisites: Read access to the source code implementing a discount/pricing calculation function. A running build of the application (or its checkout/pricing API) and an account/session capable of triggering the discount calculation to confirm the identified logic flaw at runtime.
items.whatItIs: Tracing through the actual discount calculation code shows it can produce a bigger discount than intended, apply the same discount more than once when it should only apply once, or let two discounts combine in a way the business never meant to allow.
items.rootCause: Discount logic tends to pile up special cases and interacting rules over time — percentage discounts, flat discounts, coupon stacking rules, minimum order amounts. It's easy for a specific combination of these, or a specific order they get applied in, to produce a result nobody actually intended — especially if there was never an explicit, enforced upper limit or a rule preventing certain discount types from combining.
items.impact: A customer, or an attacker posing as one, obtains a product or service far below the intended price. In the worst implementations that means free, or even a negative total where the business ends up owing money. The loss is direct and measurable, and it scales with how many times the flaw is used before anyone notices.
stepsToIdentify: Read the complete discount/pricing calculation logic, tracing exactly how multiple discount types (percentage, flat, coupon-based) interact and whether any explicit maximum-discount or mutual-exclusivity enforcement exists.

Identify specific input combinations or repeated-application sequences that the logic's structure suggests might not be correctly bounded (e.g. applying the same percentage discount function twice in a multi-step checkout flow without a check that it's already been applied).
Build and run the application (or its checkout API), then attempt the identified combination/sequence against a test cart/order to observe the resulting calculated total.
Confirm whether the resulting discount exceeds the intended maximum, or the total price is unreasonably (or impossibly, e.g. negative) low.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes business-logic testing against a running build of the reviewed application's checkout/pricing functionality, using a test account and test order.
Construct a test cart/order and apply the specific discount combination or repeated-application sequence identified via source review.
Confirm the resulting calculated total reflects the identified flaw (an excessive discount, an unintended stacking, or a negative total).
Where feasible, complete the checkout flow in a test environment to confirm the flawed price is actually charged/recorded, not just displayed transiently.
Document the exact source location of the flawed calculation logic and the confirmed runtime financial-impact evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Trace the discount-calculation function's logic for missing bounds/mutual-exclusivity checks
Attempt to apply the same discount coupon twice within a multi-step checkout flow
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/cart/apply-coupon -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"code":"SAVE20"}'
curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/cart/apply-coupon -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"code":"SAVE20"}'

examplePayloads.label: Attempt to stack two normally-mutually-exclusive discount types
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/cart/apply-coupon -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"code":"NEWUSER50"}'
curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/cart/apply-coupon -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"code":"CLEARANCE70"}'

variants: Discount-stacking flaw (two discounts that should be mutually exclusive both applying) versus a repeated-application flaw (the same single discount applied more than once via a multi-step flow lacking idempotency).

Flaw producing an excessive-but-still-positive discount versus one capable of producing a negative total, the latter being materially more severe since it could result in the business owing the customer money.
mitigation: Implement an explicit, enforced maximum total-discount cap (as a percentage or absolute amount) applied as a final validation step regardless of how many individual discounts were combined to reach that total.

Explicitly define and enforce discount-type mutual-exclusivity rules in a single, centralized location rather than relying on the order of operations across multiple, independently-written code paths to prevent unintended stacking.
Design multi-step checkout/discount-application flows to be idempotent — reapplying the same coupon/discount code should have no additional effect rather than compounding.
Include business-logic-specific test cases (discount stacking, repeated application, boundary/edge-case order values) in the standard regression-test suite for the pricing/checkout module.

links: OWASP WSTG-BUSL-01 (Test Business Logic Data Validation)

items.title: Race Condition / TOCTOU (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code implementing a check-then-act sequence on a shared resource (a balance check followed by a deduction, a stock-quantity check followed by a decrement) without adequate locking/atomicity. A running build of the application and a tool capable of firing concurrent requests (a script using threading/async, or Burp's Turbo Intruder).
items.whatItIs: Code that checks something (is there enough balance, is there enough stock) and then, as a separate later step, acts on that check (deducts the balance, reduces the stock) isn't written as one single, atomic database operation. That leaves a window where multiple requests happening at the same time can all pass the initial check based on the same not-yet-updated number, before any of them has actually applied their update — letting the action succeed more times than it should ever be allowed to.
items.rootCause: Writing a check-then-act sequence as two separate database steps (first read the current value, then separately update it) instead of one combined, atomic operation leaves a timing gap that simultaneous requests can exploit. This is a well-known, common pattern of bug, and it's directly spottable in the code by looking for exactly this separated 'check, then act later' shape applied to something shared and contested, like stock or balance.
items.impact: An attacker fires several requests at the endpoint simultaneously, so the check-then-act sequence succeeds more times than the real state should permit. That means spending more than an account holds, buying more of a limited item than exists, or redeeming a single-use coupon repeatedly. The result is direct financial loss or a break in inventory and business-logic integrity.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for a check-then-act pattern on a shared, mutable resource — a separate read (checking a balance/quantity) followed by a separate write (deducting/decrementing) rather than a single, atomic conditional update.

Confirm whether the surrounding code applies any database-level locking (a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, a transaction with an appropriate isolation level) that would close the race window despite the logically-separated check and act steps.

Build and run the application, then fire a burst of concurrent requests against the identified endpoint (using a test account with a known, limited balance/stock scenario) to test whether the race condition is practically exploitable.
Confirm whether the total effect of the concurrent requests exceeds what the resource's actual starting state should have permitted.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes concurrency/race-condition testing against a running build of the reviewed application, using a nominated test account with a controlled starting balance/stock scenario.
Set the test account/resource to a known, limited state (e.g. an account balance of exactly $10, or a single unit of limited-stock inventory).
Fire a burst of concurrent requests (10-20) against the identified check-then-act endpoint simultaneously.
Confirm whether more than the expected single successful operation occurred (e.g. multiple purchases succeeding against a single unit of stock, or the account balance going negative).
Document the exact source location of the non-atomic check-then-act pattern and the confirmed runtime race-condition exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for a separated check-then-act pattern on a shared resource
Fire concurrent requests against the vulnerable endpoint using Burp's Turbo Intruder
examplePayloads.command: # Turbo Intruder script: send 20 identical purchase requests concurrently against a test account with 1 unit of stock available

examplePayloads.label: Simple concurrent-request test via a shell loop with backgrounding
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/purchase -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"itemId":"limited-stock-item"}' & done; wait

variants: Race condition on a financial balance-deduction operation versus on a limited-stock inventory decrement — both share the same non-atomic check-then-act root cause but differ in business-impact category.
Race condition exploitable via simple, simultaneous request bursts versus requiring more precise timing manipulation (a slow-response trigger on one request to widen the race window for others).
mitigation: Replace the separated check-then-act pattern with a single, atomic database operation — a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount` that both checks and updates in one indivisible statement, relying on the database to reject the update if the condition is no longer true.

Where a more complex, multi-step operation is genuinely required, wrap it in a database transaction with an appropriate isolation level and explicit row-level locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) to serialize concurrent access to the same resource.

Apply application-level rate limiting or idempotency-key requirements on financially/inventory-sensitive endpoints as a defense-in-depth measure, reducing the practical window for race-condition abuse.
Include concurrency-specific test cases (firing concurrent requests against a resource with a known, limited starting state) in the standard security-focused regression-test suite.

links: CWE-362 (Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization)
OWASP WSTG-BUSL-04 (Test for Process Timing)

items.title: Hardcoded Encryption IV / Static Nonce Reuse
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code performing symmetric encryption (AES or similar block-cipher usage). A running build of the application (or a standalone test harness reproducing the identified encryption call) to capture and compare multiple ciphertexts for the same or related plaintext.
items.whatItIs: Looking directly at the encryption code shows it uses the exact same fixed starting value (an IV or nonce) every single time it encrypts something, instead of generating a fresh, random one for each individual encryption operation.
items.rootCause: Many encryption modes require a genuinely unique starting value for every single encryption to keep their security guarantees intact. Generating and properly storing a fresh one alongside each encrypted piece of data takes a bit more work than just reusing one convenient, hardcoded value — and the real-world consequence of reusing it isn't always obvious to someone without a deep cryptography background.
items.impact: What this costs depends on the cipher mode, and the range is wide. In CBC mode, identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, which leaks structural information about the data. In CTR and GCM modes it is far worse: an attacker observing two ciphertexts encrypted under the same key and starting value can recover the plaintext outright. In GCM specifically it can also expose the authentication key, breaking the integrity guarantee as well as confidentiality.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for encryption call sites and confirm whether the IV/nonce parameter is a literal, hardcoded value or a per-call freshly-generated one.
Where a per-call generation is used, confirm it uses a cryptographically secure random source rather than a predictable one (overlapping with the insecure-randomness finding).
Confirm the specific cipher mode in use (CBC, CTR, GCM), since the severity of IV/nonce reuse differs materially between modes.

Build and run the application (or a standalone test harness reproducing the call), encrypt several different plaintexts with the identified function, and confirm whether the same IV is indeed reused across each, and whether structural information (e.g. identical block patterns for identical plaintext blocks in CBC mode) is observably leaked.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cryptographic-analysis testing against a running build (or standalone harness) of the reviewed encryption code.
Encrypt several test plaintexts (including some sharing common substrings/blocks) using the identified function and capture the resulting ciphertexts.
Confirm the same IV is used across all captures.

For CBC mode, demonstrate the structural leak by showing identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. For CTR/GCM mode, demonstrate plaintext recovery via XOR of two ciphertexts encrypted with the same key/nonce, using known or partially-known plaintext for one of them.
Document the exact source location of the hardcoded IV/nonce and the confirmed cryptographic weakness demonstrated.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for a hardcoded IV/nonce literal in an encryption call
Encrypt two plaintexts with a shared prefix using the identified function to observe CBC block-pattern leakage
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from app.crypto import encrypt  # the identified vulnerable function
print(encrypt(b'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' + b'secret1').hex())
print(encrypt(b'AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA' + b'secret2').hex())
"

examplePayloads.label: Demonstrate plaintext recovery via ciphertext XOR under nonce reuse (CTR/GCM-style stream cipher)
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
c1 = bytes.fromhex('<ciphertext1>')
c2 = bytes.fromhex('<ciphertext2>')
xor = bytes(a ^ b for a, b in zip(c1, c2))  # equals plaintext1 XOR plaintext2 under nonce reuse
print(xor)
"

variants: Hardcoded IV in CBC mode (structural, block-level leakage) versus a hardcoded/reused nonce in CTR or GCM mode (full plaintext-recovery and, for GCM, authentication-key-recovery risk) — the latter is materially more severe.

IV/nonce reuse across every encryption operation globally versus reuse limited to a specific, narrower context (e.g. only when re-encrypting the same record) that still enables a related-plaintext attack in that narrower scope.
mitigation: Generate a fresh, cryptographically random IV/nonce for every single encryption operation, using a CSPRNG, and store/transmit it alongside the resulting ciphertext (IVs don't need to be secret, only unique).
For GCM specifically, ensure the nonce is never reused with the same key under any circumstance, given the severe authentication-key-recovery consequence of GCM nonce reuse.
Use a well-maintained, high-level cryptographic library that handles IV/nonce generation and management correctly by default, rather than manually managing this parameter.
Add a static-analysis rule flagging any hardcoded IV/nonce literal passed to an encryption call as a mandatory code-review blocker.

links: CWE-323 (Reusing a Nonce, Key Pair in Encryption)
NIST SP 800-38D (Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode)

items.title: Insecure Randomness
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code generating a value that requires unpredictability for a security purpose (a password-reset token, a session identifier, an API key). A running build of the application to collect a sample of generated values for statistical validation of the source-level finding.
items.whatItIs: Code that generates something security-sensitive uses an everyday, non-cryptographic random function, or builds the value from predictable pieces like a timestamp or a simple counter, instead of using a proper cryptographically secure random generator. This is confirmed directly by finding the exact line generating the value and checking which method it actually uses.
items.rootCause: Everyday random functions are simpler to use and perfectly fine for things that don't need real security, like test data or animations. It's easy to overlook the difference between 'random enough for general use' and 'genuinely unpredictable' when a developer just reaches for a familiar function without realizing the specific value being generated actually matters for security.
items.impact: An attacker who works out the generator's algorithm and its starting value can predict other values it produces. Whatever security property depended on those values being unguessable is then gone. In practice that means forging password-reset tokens that look valid, predicting session identifiers to hijack accounts, or guessing API keys issued to other users.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for every generation call site producing a value later used for a security purpose (tokens, session IDs, API keys, one-time codes) and identify the specific randomness API used at each.
Confirm whether each is a cryptographically secure generator or a standard, non-cryptographic one.
Where a CSPRNG is used, confirm it isn't seeded with a predictable value.

Build and run the application, collect a sample of generated values for a representative, security-relevant use case, and statistically analyze them for patterns consistent with the weak generator identified in source.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes value-sample collection and predictability analysis against a running build of the reviewed application.
Extract or replicate the exact generation algorithm and seeding logic identified in source.
Collect a representative sample of generated values (for test accounts/requests).
Attempt to reconstruct the generator's state from the sample and predict a subsequent value.
Confirm the predicted value is accepted as valid by the application, demonstrating practical exploitability.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for non-cryptographic randomness in a security-sensitive generation context
Collect a sample of generated password-reset tokens for test accounts
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/password-reset -d '{"email":"test'$i'@example.com"}'; done

examplePayloads.label: Statistically test collected values for predictability

variants: Weak randomness affecting a password-reset token specifically (directly enabling account takeover) versus a lower-stakes value like a non-security-relevant UI identifier that happens to use the same weak, shared utility function.
A cryptographically-appropriate generator undermined by a predictable seed, rather than the generator choice itself being the flaw.
mitigation: Use a cryptographically secure random number generator for every security-sensitive value, without exception.
Never seed a CSPRNG with a predictable value; rely on the platform's own properly-sourced entropy for seeding.
Audit the codebase for every randomness-generation call site as part of a security-focused code review, tagging and consistently treating every security-relevant use with the correct API.
Ensure generated tokens/identifiers carry sufficient length/entropy (128 bits or more) regardless of the specific generator chosen.

links: CWE-338 (Use of Cryptographically Weak PRNG)

items.title: Weak Cryptography (Algorithm/Mode)
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code performing encryption or hashing. Standard cryptographic-analysis knowledge to recognize deprecated/weak algorithm and mode names in the code (DES, RC4, MD5, ECB mode).
items.whatItIs: The application uses an outdated or broken encryption method or hashing algorithm — like DES or RC4 (both considered broken for any real security purpose today), ECB mode (which doesn't hide repeating patterns in the data), or MD5/SHA-1 for anything security-related (both known to have real, practical weaknesses, though still fine for basic, non-adversarial integrity checks). This is confirmed by looking directly at the code where the algorithm gets chosen.
items.rootCause: A weak or outdated algorithm was likely chosen back when the code was first written — maybe it seemed fine at the time, or it was just the first, familiar option available — and it was never revisited or upgraded since. Sometimes a library's own default setting quietly picks a weaker option than the developer realized, simply because they didn't explicitly specify a stronger one.
