items.impact: The consequence depends on which weak algorithm or mode is in use. With ECB mode, patterns in the data remain visible in the ciphertext, revealing structure. With genuinely broken algorithms it goes further: DES has a key space small enough to search, RC4 leaks statistical biases, and MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collision attacks that break any scheme relying on collision resistance, such as a digital signature.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for cryptographic algorithm/mode selection strings or constants (`DES`, `RC4`, `ECB`, `MD5`, `SHA1`) in any encryption or hashing call.

For each identified use, confirm the specific security property the code relies on that algorithm/mode for (confidentiality, integrity, collision-resistance) to assess whether the specific weakness is actually relevant to that use case.

Where ECB mode is identified for encrypting data with repeating structure (an image, a structured record), build and run the application to encrypt a representative sample and visually/statistically confirm the pattern-leakage is observable in the resulting ciphertext.

Where MD5/SHA-1 is used for a genuinely collision-resistance-dependent purpose (a digital signature, a deduplication scheme relying on uniqueness), assess the practical feasibility of a collision attack in that specific context.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cryptographic-analysis testing against a running build (or standalone harness) of the reviewed encryption/hashing code.

For an ECB-mode finding, encrypt a representative, patterned test plaintext (e.g. a bitmap image, or repeating structured data) using the identified function and visually/statistically confirm the pattern-leakage in the resulting ciphertext.

For a DES/RC4 finding, demonstrate the algorithm's known practical weakness (a brute-forceable key space for DES, known keystream-bias-based plaintext recovery techniques for RC4) against a sample ciphertext.
For an MD5/SHA-1 collision-resistance-dependent finding, where practical, demonstrate a collision using publicly available collision-generation techniques/tools for the specific hash.
Document the exact source location of the weak algorithm/mode selection and the confirmed practical weakness demonstrated.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for deprecated/weak algorithm and mode selection
Demonstrate ECB-mode pattern leakage by encrypting a structured test plaintext
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
from app.crypto import ecb_encrypt  # the identified vulnerable function
result = ecb_encrypt(b'BLOCK1BLOCK1BLOCK1BLOCK1' + b'DIFFERENT_BLOCK_')
print(result.hex())  # observe identical ciphertext for identical 'BLOCK1' plaintext blocks
"

examplePayloads.label: Check for a feasible MD5 collision in a collision-resistance-dependent use case
examplePayloads.command: # use a public MD5-collision-generation tool (e.g. hashclash) to produce two distinct inputs sharing the same MD5 hash, relevant if the application relies on MD5 uniqueness for integrity/dedup purposes

variants: ECB mode used for encrypting genuinely structured, pattern-rich data (high real-world impact from visible leakage) versus for data with little inherent structure (lower, though still present, real-world impact).

MD5/SHA-1 used purely for non-adversarial checksumming (lower practical risk) versus used in a context genuinely relying on collision-resistance against an adversary (a digital-signature or certificate-related use, high practical risk).
mitigation: Replace DES/RC4 with a current, strong algorithm (AES-256) for any encryption use.
Replace ECB mode with an authenticated mode (GCM) or, at minimum, CBC with a properly random, unique IV per operation (see the related IV-reuse finding for correct IV handling).

Replace MD5/SHA-1 with SHA-256 or stronger for any hashing use where collision-resistance genuinely matters; for password hashing specifically, use a dedicated password-hashing function (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) rather than a general-purpose cryptographic hash at all.

Add a static-analysis rule flagging any use of a deprecated algorithm/mode name as a mandatory code-review blocker, and periodically audit the codebase for cryptographic-primitive currency against current guidance.

links: NIST SP 800-131A (Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths)
CWE-326 (Inadequate Encryption Strength)

items.title: Insecure File Upload Handling (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the file-upload-handling source code (distinct from SRC-002's Content-Type-trust focus, this item covers the broader handling: storage location, filename handling, and execution prevention). A running build of the application and an HTTP client to confirm the identified handling gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: Tracing the file-upload code end to end reveals one or more gaps. Uploaded files may be stored somewhere the web server will execute them. The uploaded filename may not be cleaned up, letting traversal characters or dangerous extensions pass through unchanged. Or there may be no limit at all on file size, type, or how many files one person can upload.
items.rootCause: Handling file uploads securely requires several separate, deliberate protections — storing files outside the publicly web-servable area, cleaning up filenames, blocking execution at the storage location, and setting size/type/count limits. It's common for one or more of these individual protections to be missing even when others are present, since each one guards against a different risk, and there's no single, obvious 'is this upload secure' check that catches every gap at once.
items.impact: Which control is missing decides the outcome. An unsanitised filename allows path traversal, writing a file outside the intended folder and potentially overwriting something sensitive. A script file stored somewhere the web server will execute gives direct remote code execution. And with no limit on file size or count, it becomes a denial of service.
stepsToIdentify: Trace the complete file-upload-handling code path: how is the filename derived and sanitized (if at all), where is the file stored relative to the web-servable root, and what (if any) size/type/count limits are enforced.
Confirm whether the storage location is configured to prevent script execution (via web-server configuration) independent of what the application code itself does.
Build and run the application, then attempt to upload a file with a path-traversal-crafted filename (`../../etc/test_poc`) and confirm whether it's written outside the intended directory.
Separately, attempt to upload and then access a script-type file to confirm whether the storage location actually executes it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes file-upload handling testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Attempt a path-traversal-crafted filename upload and confirm the resulting file's actual storage location.
Attempt to upload a script-type file (appropriate to the identified server-side language) and access it via its resulting URL to check for execution.
Where size/count limits are found absent in source, submit an oversized or high-count upload as a bounded, authorized test to confirm the absence at runtime.
Document the exact source location of each missing control and the confirmed runtime impact for each.

examplePayloads.label: Trace the upload-handling code path for filename sanitization and storage-location logic
Attempt a path-traversal filename upload
Attempt upload and execution of a script-type file

variants: Path-traversal-vulnerable filename handling versus execution-permitting storage location — these are distinct, independent gaps that may exist together or separately.
Missing size/count limits enabling a storage-exhaustion denial-of-service, distinct from the code-execution/traversal-focused variants.
mitigation: Sanitize uploaded filenames strictly (strip path-traversal sequences, generate a new, random server-side filename rather than trusting the client-supplied one at all).
Store uploaded files outside the web-servable root, or in a location explicitly configured (at the web-server level, not just the application level) to never execute scripts.
Enforce explicit maximum file size, allowed file-type, and per-user/per-timeframe upload-count limits.
Combine with independent content-type verification (see the related Content-Type-trust finding) for complete, defense-in-depth upload security.

links: CWE-22 (Path Traversal)
OWASP WSTG-BUSL-09 (Test Upload of Unexpected File Types)

items.title: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Data
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code responsible for storing sensitive data (credentials, PII, financial data) to a database, file, or cache. A running build of the application and direct access to its backing data store (a test database, cache instance) to confirm the identified storage format at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The code that stores sensitive data — a password, a card number, personal information — writes it in plain, readable text (or something trivially reversible), instead of applying proper protection first: real password hashing for credentials, or actual encryption for other sensitive fields. This is confirmed directly by finding the storage code and checking whether any protective step happens before the write.
items.rootCause: Actually protecting sensitive data at rest requires a deliberate extra step — hashing or encrypting it — beyond just writing the value to storage. This step sometimes gets skipped during early development just to get something working, or applied inconsistently as new sensitive fields get added to the system over time without anyone going back to check them all.
items.impact: Anyone who gains read access to the data store obtains the sensitive data directly, in plain text or a form trivially reversed. They might arrive through a separate vulnerability such as SQL injection or an exposed backup, through insider access, or via a leaked database dump. No additional protective layer stands in the way, because the application never applied one.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every code path writing sensitive data (credentials, PII, payment data) to persistent storage, and confirm whether any hashing/encryption transformation is applied immediately before the write.
For credential storage specifically, confirm whether a proper, dedicated password-hashing function (bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2) is used, versus a general-purpose hash or, worse, no transformation at all.

Build and run the application, populate representative test data, then directly inspect the backing data store to confirm the actual stored format matches (or contradicts) what the source code review indicated.

Cross-reference which specific sensitive fields lack protection versus which are correctly protected, since this is commonly an inconsistent, partial gap rather than a uniform absence across every field.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes direct data-store inspection of a test environment populated with representative sensitive test data.
Populate the application with test sensitive data (a test account's password, test PII fields) through normal use.
Directly query the backing data store and inspect the stored representation of each sensitive field.
Confirm which fields are stored in plaintext or trivially-reversible form, distinct from any correctly hashed/encrypted fields.
Document the exact source location of each unprotected storage call and the confirmed plaintext/reversible storage format observed.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for credential/PII storage without a hashing/encryption transformation
Directly inspect the test database for stored credential format
examplePayloads.command: mysql -h test-db -u test -p -e "SELECT password FROM users WHERE email='test@example.com';"

variants: Credentials stored in plaintext (most severe, direct account-takeover risk for every affected account if the store is ever exposed) versus stored with a fast, general-purpose hash (MD5/SHA-256) rather than a proper, slow password-hashing function.
PII/financial data stored without at-rest encryption, distinct from credential-specific hashing concerns.
mitigation: Hash all credentials using a dedicated, slow password-hashing function (bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) with an appropriate work factor, never a general-purpose fast hash or plaintext storage.
Encrypt all other genuinely sensitive data at rest (PII, financial data) using a properly-managed key, per the guidance in the related key-management finding.

Conduct a systematic, field-by-field data-model review specifically for sensitive-data-protection consistency, since new fields added later commonly miss the protection convention established for older ones.
Add a static-analysis rule or code-review checklist item flagging any new sensitive-data-model field for a mandatory storage-protection review before merge.

links: CWE-916 (Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort)
OWASP WSTG-CRYP-04 (Testing for Weak Encryption)

items.title: Missing Server-Side Validation Duplicated from Client-Side Only
items.prerequisites: Read access to both client-side (JavaScript) and server-side validation code for the same business rule/input field. A running build of the application and an HTTP client (Burp Suite) capable of bypassing the client entirely to submit requests directly to the server.
items.whatItIs: A business rule or input check — like a maximum quantity, or a required format — only exists in the JavaScript running in the browser. The server-side code accepts whatever gets submitted with no independent double-check of its own. This is confirmed directly by finding the validation logic in the client-side code and finding nothing matching it on the server side for the same endpoint.
items.rootCause: Client-side checks get added because they give instant feedback without a round-trip to the server, which is genuinely good for user experience. But it's a common and serious mistake to assume that check is enough — forgetting that anyone can fully control what their own browser sends, and can easily skip that check using developer tools or by calling the API directly. The server, which the user can't control, is the only place a check can actually be trusted to have happened.
items.impact: An attacker bypasses the client entirely — disabling JavaScript, editing the request through a proxy, or calling the API directly — and submits whatever value the client-side check would have refused. The server processes it as though it were valid. What that costs depends on what the rule was protecting: a quantity limit, a price field, or a flag governing access. It ranges from a data-quality annoyance to a serious security bypass.
stepsToIdentify: For each significant business rule/validation constraint found in client-side JavaScript, search the corresponding server-side endpoint handler for an equivalent, independent validation check.
Flag any rule present client-side but with no server-side counterpart at all.

Build and run the application, then bypass the client-side check (via a direct API call using Burp/curl, skipping the browser and its JavaScript entirely) and observe whether the server processes the otherwise-blocked value.
Assess the specific impact of each confirmed gap based on what the bypassed rule was meant to enforce.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes client-bypass testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Identify the specific client-side-only validation rule and its corresponding server-side endpoint.
Construct a direct API request violating the rule (an out-of-range quantity, a malformed value) and submit it, bypassing the client entirely.
Confirm the server accepts and processes the otherwise-invalid value.
Document the exact source location of the missing server-side validation and the confirmed impact of the bypass.

examplePayloads.label: Identify a client-side-only validation rule in JavaScript
Confirm no equivalent server-side check exists for the same field
Submit a direct API request bypassing the client-side-only check

variants: Missing server-side validation of a business-logic constraint (a quantity/price limit) versus of a basic input-format constraint (an email format, a required field) — the former typically carries more direct business impact.
Client-side check entirely absent server-side, versus present but implemented inconsistently/more permissively than the client-side version (a partial, rather than complete, gap).
mitigation: Implement every significant validation rule and business constraint server-side as the authoritative enforcement point, treating client-side validation purely as a user-experience convenience that provides no actual security or data-integrity guarantee.
Adopt a policy/checklist requiring every client-side validation rule to have a documented, verified server-side equivalent before the corresponding feature is considered complete.
Include a systematic client-bypass test pass (submitting requests directly to the API for every significant client-side-validated field) as part of the standard security-focused test suite.
Never assume a request originated from, or was constrained by, the official client application; treat every server-side input as fully untrusted regardless of its apparent origin.

links: OWASP WSTG-BUSL-01 (Test Business Logic Data Validation)

items.title: Cross-Site Scripting (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to view-rendering source code (templates, front-end component code) that outputs user-controllable data. A running build of the application and a browser (or curl for reflected-response confirmation) to confirm the identified injection point at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The application puts user-controlled data — a URL parameter, a saved profile field, a comment — directly into a web page without properly escaping it for the specific spot it ends up in (inside the page body, inside an HTML attribute, inside a script, inside a link). This is confirmed directly by finding the rendering code and seeing that the templating system's automatic escaping is turned off, bypassed, or just never applied for that specific spot.
items.rootCause: Most modern templating tools automatically escape output by default, but a developer can explicitly turn that protection off for one specific value — often because that value is expected to contain some real, intended HTML, like a rich-text field — without properly cleaning it up first. Or a lower-level piece of code (directly injecting content into the page via JavaScript) skips the templating system's protection entirely.
items.impact: An attacker who controls the unescaped value can inject HTML or JavaScript that runs for anyone viewing the page. They may supply it directly through a URL parameter, or indirectly through a stored field such as a profile bio or comment that is later shown to other users. From there they can steal session cookies, harvest credentials with a fake login prompt, or do anything else the victim's authenticated session permits.
stepsToIdentify: Search templates/rendering code for explicit "raw"/"safe"/unescaped output directives, and for direct DOM-manipulation calls (`innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `document.write`) that bypass a templating engine's auto-escaping.
For each identified location, trace the rendered value back to confirm it's genuinely user-controllable (directly or via stored data from another user).

Build and run the application, then submit a benign, verifiable script payload (an alert or a request to a controlled listener) to the identified input and observe whether it executes when the affected page is rendered.
Where the value is stored and rendered to other users (a profile field, a comment), confirm the payload persists and executes for a separate viewing session, distinguishing stored from reflected XSS.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes XSS testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Submit a benign, verifiable script payload to the identified vulnerable input.
Load the page where the value is rendered and confirm the payload executes.
For a stored-XSS case, confirm the payload persists and executes when viewed from a separate session/account.
Document the exact source location of the missing/bypassed output encoding and the confirmed runtime script execution.

examplePayloads.label: Search templates for explicit unescaped/raw output directives
Submit a benign, verifiable script payload to the identified input
Confirm stored-XSS execution from a separate viewing session
examplePayloads.command: # visit the affected profile page from a different browser/session and confirm the callback fires

variants: Stored XSS (the payload persists in the data store and executes for every subsequent viewer) versus reflected XSS (the payload is present only in the immediate request/response and requires the victim to click a crafted link).
XSS via an explicit "safe"/raw templating directive versus via direct client-side DOM manipulation (`innerHTML`) that bypasses the templating engine's protection entirely.
mitigation: Rely on the templating engine's default auto-escaping for all user-controllable output; avoid "raw"/"safe"/unescaped output directives unless the value has been rigorously sanitized through a dedicated HTML-sanitization library first.

Where rich-text/HTML content genuinely needs to be rendered from user input, sanitize it through a well-maintained, allowlist-based HTML sanitizer (DOMPurify or an equivalent) rather than trusting it directly.

Avoid direct DOM manipulation (`innerHTML`) with user-controllable data in client-side JavaScript; use safe, text-only DOM APIs (`textContent`) or the framework's own safe-rendering mechanisms instead.
Apply a strict Content-Security-Policy as a defense-in-depth layer, limiting the impact of any XSS that does slip through despite output-encoding controls.

links: CWE-116 (Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output)
OWASP WSTG-INPV-01 (Testing for Reflected Cross Site Scripting)

items.title: Dangerous Function / API Usage
items.prerequisites: Read access to the full application source code and its list of imported libraries/dependencies. Standard string-search tooling (grep/ripgrep) to locate calls to specific, known-dangerous functions.
items.whatItIs: The codebase calls a function that's well known to be dangerous when fed untrusted input — something that runs arbitrary code from a text string, an old-style C function that copies text with no length checking, or a function that runs shell commands built from user input. This is confirmed directly by finding that specific function call and tracing whether its input can actually come from an untrusted source.
items.rootCause: Certain functions in most languages are well documented as unsafe for particular kinds of input — unbounded copying with no length check, or running a text string as code. They remain available regardless. They get used out of convenience, or unfamiliarity with the safer alternative, without the developer fully recognising how dangerous that specific use is.
items.impact: The consequence depends on the specific function and how it is used, ranging from a buffer overflow with unbounded native string functions to arbitrary code execution where a dynamic evaluation function receives attacker-influenced input. This finding is best read as a root cause rather than a final answer. Trace the function's input back to its source and it usually resolves into something more specific: command injection, template injection, or a memory-safety bug.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for calls to well-known dangerous functions for the specific language in use (`eval`, `exec`, `strcpy`, `gets`, `Function()` constructor with a string argument).
For each call found, trace its input parameter back to confirm whether it can be influenced, directly or indirectly, by untrusted (user-supplied) data.

Where the input is confirmed attacker-influenceable, classify the specific resulting vulnerability class (code injection if it's a dynamic-evaluation function, buffer overflow if it's an unbounded native string function) and cross-reference with the more specific, dedicated finding for that class.

Where the function is called only with fully fixed, developer-controlled input (no untrusted influence), note it as a lower-priority hygiene/best-practice finding rather than a directly exploitable one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes exploitation testing for the specific vulnerability class identified as reachable through the dangerous function call.
Follow the exploitation steps documented in the corresponding, more specific finding (command injection, SSTI, buffer overflow) that this dangerous-function usage enables.

Where the dangerous function's usage doesn't map cleanly to an existing, more specific finding category, independently confirm exploitability by crafting an input designed to trigger the function's known-dangerous behavior and observing the resulting impact.
Document the exact source location of the dangerous function call and its confirmed (or assessed-absent, if input isn't actually attacker-influenceable) exploitability.

Recommend replacing the dangerous function with a safe, purpose-built equivalent (parameterized queries instead of dynamic SQL construction, bounded string functions instead of unbounded ones) rather than attempting to sanitize input ahead of the dangerous call.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for well-known dangerous function calls
Trace a flagged eval() call's input back to a request parameter
Confirm exploitability with a benign proof-of-concept input

variants: A dynamic-code-evaluation function (`eval`) fed attacker-influenceable input, a direct code-injection precursor, versus an unbounded native string-copy function (`strcpy`) in a lower-level language, a buffer-overflow precursor.

The dangerous function called with fully fixed, non-attacker-influenceable input (a hygiene finding, not directly exploitable) versus with confirmed, traceable untrusted input (a directly exploitable finding).
mitigation: Eliminate use of `eval()`/dynamic-code-evaluation functions on any string that could ever contain untrusted input; use a safe, purpose-built parser (a math-expression evaluator library, a JSON parser) for the specific legitimate use case instead.
Replace unbounded native string functions with their bounds-checked equivalents (`strlcpy`, `fgets`) throughout the codebase.

Add a static-analysis (SAST) rule flagging any use of a known-dangerous function as a mandatory code-review item, requiring explicit justification and confirmation of non-attacker-influenceable input if the call must remain.
Where source access allows, conduct a periodic, dedicated sweep for dangerous-function usage as part of routine secure-code-review practice, not just during external assessments.

links: CWE-95 (Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code)
CWE-120 (Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input)

items.title: Improper Error/Exception Handling
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's error/exception-handling source code, particularly a global/top-level error handler. A running build of the application and an HTTP client to trigger a representative unhandled error condition and confirm the identified handling gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: When something goes wrong, the application's error-handling code sends the raw error details straight back to the user — a full stack trace, an internal file path, a database error revealing table structure — instead of a generic, safe message. This is confirmed by finding the code that handles unexpected errors and checking exactly what detail it includes in the response sent to the user.
items.rootCause: A generic error handler that just returns whatever error it caught is a common, quick way to build things during development, since it's genuinely useful for debugging. It's easy for that same behavior to get left in place once the app goes live, either because nobody specifically went back to change it for production, or because the framework's own default behavior is verbose unless someone explicitly configures it not to be.
items.impact: Verbose errors hand an attacker the internal detail they need to plan the next step. A stack trace reveals exact framework and library versions, which turns a broad search for vulnerabilities into a targeted one. Internal file paths expose the server's directory structure. Database errors reveal table and column names that make SQL injection far easier to aim. Occasionally the leaked detail is sensitive in itself, such as a connection string inside an exception message.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the application's global/top-level error handler and confirm exactly what detail it includes in the response sent to the client for an unhandled exception.

Confirm whether the handler's verbose behavior is gated by an environment/configuration flag (development vs. production mode), and if so, whether the production environment is confirmed to actually have that flag set correctly.

Build and run the application in its production configuration, then trigger a representative unhandled-error condition (malformed input designed to cause an exception rather than a graceful validation rejection) and inspect the actual response.
Confirm whether the response includes a stack trace, internal file paths, or raw database error content.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes error-triggering testing against a running build of the reviewed application, in its production (or production-equivalent) configuration.
Craft an input designed to trigger an unhandled exception at the specific code path identified via source review.
Submit the crafted input and inspect the resulting error response for verbose detail.
Where a leaked detail reveals a specific library version, cross-reference it against known CVEs for that version as a potential escalation path.
Document the exact source location of the verbose error handler and the specific detail confirmed leaked in the runtime response.

examplePayloads.label: Locate the global error handler and its response-construction logic
examplePayloads.command: grep -rn 'app.use((err\|@ExceptionHandler\|except Exception as e' src/ | grep -A5 'stack\|traceback'

examplePayloads.label: Trigger a representative unhandled exception with malformed input
Trigger a database-level exception via a crafted, unexpected value

variants: Verbose error handling present unconditionally regardless of environment, versus correctly gated by a development/production flag but the production environment's flag is misconfigured/left at the development default.

Leaked stack trace/file-path detail (reconnaissance-value information disclosure) versus a leaked raw database error/connection string (potentially directly sensitive data disclosure) — the latter is materially more severe.
mitigation: Configure a global error handler that returns a generic, non-verbose error message and appropriate status code to the client in production, logging the full exception detail server-side only, never in the client-facing response.
Verify the production environment's configuration flag is correctly set to disable verbose/development-mode error output, as a deployment-checklist item rather than an assumption.
Apply the generic-error-response behavior consistently across every error type (validation errors, unhandled exceptions, database errors) rather than only the most obviously anticipated ones.
Include a test case in the CI pipeline that triggers a representative unhandled exception against a production-configured build and asserts the response contains no verbose detail.

links: CWE-209 (Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information)
OWASP WSTG-ERRH-01 (Testing for Improper Error Handling)

items.title: Improper Input Validation
items.prerequisites: Read access to input-handling source code across a representative set of endpoints. A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the identified validation gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: One or more input fields accept and process data without properly checking its type, length, format, or range first. This is confirmed by finding the code that handles that input and seeing that there's no validation logic there at all, or that what's there is incomplete or inconsistent.
items.rootCause: Input checking has to be deliberately built for every single input, and it's common for a specific field or endpoint to just not have it — especially ones that feel internal or less obviously reachable by an attacker. Sometimes checking exists for the 'normal' expected input, but was never actually tested against the full range of weird, malformed, or edge-case values a real attacker might send.
items.impact: Where the unchecked input ends up decides the outcome, which ranges from crashes and instability to specific, more serious classes such as path traversal, injection, or a business-logic bypass. Treat this as a root cause rather than the final answer. Trace where the input actually flows and it usually resolves into a more specific finding with its own remediation.
stepsToIdentify: For each significant input field/endpoint, trace whether validation logic (type, length, format, range checks) exists before the input is used in any downstream processing.
Where validation exists, assess its completeness — does it correctly reject all malformed/boundary values, or only the most obviously incorrect ones.

Build and run the application, then submit a range of malformed/boundary test values (oversized strings, unexpected types, null bytes, boundary numeric values) to the identified fields and observe the resulting behavior.
Trace where the unvalidated input flows to determine the specific resulting vulnerability class (a database query, a file path, a template) for more targeted follow-up testing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes malformed-input testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Submit a systematic range of malformed/boundary values to the identified fields.
Observe and document any unexpected behavior (a crash, an unhandled exception, an unintended action).
Where the unvalidated input flows into a more specific, dangerous sink, escalate testing toward that specific finding class.
Document the exact source location of each missing/incomplete validation and the resulting impact observed.

examplePayloads.label: Trace an endpoint's input handling for validation logic
Submit a range of boundary/malformed test values
examplePayloads.command: for val in '' 'null' '-1' '99999999999999999999' '<script>' '../../etc/passwd'; do curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/api/orders -d '{"quantity":"'$val'"}'; done

variants: Missing validation on a numeric/boundary field enabling a downstream logic error, versus missing validation on a string field enabling a downstream injection vulnerability — the same root cause manifests differently depending on the field's downstream use.
Validation present but inconsistently applied across similar endpoints (one properly validates, a near-identical one added later doesn't).
mitigation: Apply strict, allowlist-based input validation (expected type, length, character set, range) at every input surface, consistently across every endpoint handling similar data.
Reject invalid input outright with a clear, safe error rather than attempting to sanitize/normalize and proceed.
Use a schema-validation library/framework applied consistently across the API rather than ad hoc, per-endpoint validation logic, reducing the chance of a missed or inconsistent check.
Include boundary and malformed-input test cases in the standard regression-test suite for every significant input field.

links: CWE-1284 (Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input)

items.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to an endpoint handler accepting an object identifier. A running build of the application and valid credentials/tokens for at least two separate test accounts to confirm the identified missing-ownership-check gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: Code handling a request that includes an item's ID looks up or changes that item using only the ID, with nothing anywhere in that code checking whether the ID actually belongs to the person making the request. This is confirmed directly by finding the data-lookup code and seeing there's no filter tying it back to the logged-in user's own account.
items.rootCause: The code correctly checks that the caller is logged in, but underneath that, the actual database lookup or update is done using only the item's ID, with no extra condition connecting it to who's actually asking. This is directly, plainly visible just by reading the code — there's no 'does this belong to the current user' check anywhere in the query.
items.impact: Any logged-in user can read or change another user's data by swapping one object identifier in an otherwise ordinary request. This is consistently the most common and most damaging vulnerability class found in both source review and black-box API testing, largely because it is trivial to automate across every account the application serves.
stepsToIdentify: For each endpoint accepting an object identifier, trace the data-access call (a database query, an ORM call) and confirm whether it includes an ownership-scoping condition tying the query to the authenticated caller's own identity.
Flag any handler where the query/update is scoped only by the supplied object ID, with no ownership condition anywhere in the call chain.
Build and run the application, then confirm the finding at runtime using two separate test accounts as described in the exploitation steps.
Check whether object identifiers are sequential/predictable, compounding the finding's practical severity if so.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-account object-access testing using the provided test accounts against the identified endpoint.
Using test account A, perform a normal action referencing one of its own object IDs.
Using test account B's token, replay the request substituting account A's object ID.
Confirm the response returns/modifies account A's data despite being authenticated as account B.
Document the exact source location of the missing ownership-scoping condition and the confirmed runtime cross-account access.

examplePayloads.label: Trace a handler's data-access query for a missing ownership-scoping condition
Confirm the missing check at runtime with two test accounts
examplePayloads.command: curl -s https://app.target.com/orders/1001 -H "Authorization: Bearer <account-B-token>"  # account A's order ID, requested as account B

variants: Missing ownership check on a read operation versus a write/delete operation, the latter being materially more severe.
Missing check identified in a REST handler versus a GraphQL resolver, the latter being easier to overlook given the spread of authorization logic across many individual resolvers.
mitigation: Add an explicit ownership-scoping condition to every data-access query/update involving a caller-supplied object identifier, scoping it to the authenticated caller's own records.

Apply a centralized, reusable authorization-check pattern (a data-access-layer wrapper enforcing ownership scoping by default) rather than requiring every individual handler to remember to add the condition manually.
Use non-sequential, non-guessable object identifiers (UUIDs) as defense in depth.
Include a static-analysis rule or code-review checklist item specifically flagging any new data-access call using a caller-supplied ID without an accompanying ownership condition.

links: OWASP API Security Top 10 - API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization
CWE-862 (Missing Authorization)

items.title: Mass Assignment / Auto-Binding (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to a create/update endpoint's request-binding code (how the request body is mapped onto the underlying data model/ORM object). A running build of the application and a valid test account's authentication token to confirm the identified auto-binding gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: A piece of code that handles creating or updating something takes the entire incoming request and automatically applies it to the underlying data record, using a framework shortcut, without an explicit list restricting which fields are actually allowed to be set this way. This is confirmed by finding that exact binding call and seeing it passes the whole, unfiltered request instead of a specifically-built, narrower set of fields.
items.rootCause: Automatically mapping a request onto a data record is a common framework convenience meant to save typing. Using it with the full, unfiltered request changes what that convenience costs. Every field on the record becomes settable by anyone who includes it, not only the fields this particular action was supposed to permit.
items.impact: A caller can raise their own privileges by setting a role or permission field. They can alter business-critical values such as a price, a balance or a status flag directly. Any field present in the underlying data model is reachable, regardless of which fields the real interface treats as editable.
stepsToIdentify: For each create/update endpoint, locate the request-binding call and confirm whether it passes the complete request body directly to the model, or an explicitly-constructed, allowlisted subset.
Where the complete body is bound directly, obtain the full underlying model schema to identify additional fields beyond the endpoint's documented/intended request structure.
Build and run the application, then craft a request including an additional field (a role, a price) alongside the legitimate expected fields and submit it using a test account.
Confirm whether the additional field was silently accepted and applied by retrieving the resulting object afterward.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes mass-assignment testing using the provided test account against the identified endpoint.
Capture the legitimate request body structure for a normal create/update action.
Add an additional, normally-restricted field to the request body.
Submit the modified request, then retrieve the resulting object to confirm whether the injected field was applied.
Document the exact source location of the unfiltered binding call and the confirmed runtime privilege-escalation or business-logic-manipulation impact.

examplePayloads.label: Locate an unfiltered auto-binding call in source
Attempt mass assignment by including an additional, restricted field
Confirm whether the injected field was applied

variants: Mass assignment enabling direct privilege escalation (a role field) versus business-logic manipulation (a price/balance field).
Vulnerable auto-binding on a create/registration endpoint (allowing a brand-new account to be created with elevated privileges) versus on an update endpoint modifying an existing account.
mitigation: Explicitly allowlist the specific fields permitted for each create/update endpoint, binding only those fields from the request body rather than passing the complete body to the framework's automatic-binding feature.

Use a dedicated, narrower input schema/DTO per endpoint reflecting exactly what that specific operation should be allowed to set, never exposing the full underlying data model directly to request-binding logic.
Apply the same allowlisting discipline consistently to every create/update endpoint for every object type.
Add a static-analysis rule flagging any use of a framework's unfiltered, complete-request-body auto-binding feature as a mandatory code-review item.

links: OWASP API Security Top 10 - API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization

items.title: Missing Integrity Verification (Updates/Artifacts)
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application/artifact update or download-and-execute code path. A running build of the application (or the specific updater component) and the ability to substitute a controlled response for the download step, to confirm the identified missing integrity check at runtime.
items.whatItIs: Code that downloads something external — a plugin, an update, a script — and then runs or loads it does so without ever checking a cryptographic signature to confirm it's genuine first. This is confirmed by finding the download-and-run code path and seeing there's no signature check anywhere between the download finishing and the file actually being used.
items.rootCause: Adding a real signature check takes deliberate extra work — embedding a trusted key, and checking the downloaded file against it before using it. That step is easy to skip if the download source is just assumed to always be legitimate, protected only by a normal secure connection — which protects the data in transit, but says nothing about whether the source itself is trustworthy or whether the download could have been swapped somewhere along the way.
items.impact: An attacker who can intercept or redirect the download delivers a malicious artefact instead of the genuine one. They might do that from a position on the network, by compromising the distribution server or CDN, or through DNS redirection. The application then loads and runs it with its own trust and privilege level, which means full compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every code path that downloads an external artifact and subsequently executes or loads it (a plugin system, an auto-updater, a dynamically-fetched script/config).
Confirm whether any cryptographic signature-verification step exists between the download and the artifact's use, distinct from simply checking that the download completed successfully over TLS.

Build and run the application (or the specific updater component), then substitute an alternate artifact in place of the legitimate download (via a test proxy or a redirected download URL) and observe whether the application proceeds to execute/load it.
Where a checksum (rather than a cryptographic signature) is the only check present, confirm it provides no real protection by recomputing a matching checksum for the substituted artifact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes download-substitution testing against a running build of the reviewed application's update/artifact-loading mechanism.
Prepare a benign, clearly-labeled proof-of-concept artifact to substitute for the legitimate download.
Intercept or redirect the download step and deliver the substitute artifact.
Confirm whether the application proceeds to execute/load the substituted artifact without any signature-verification rejection.
Document the exact source location of the missing integrity check and the confirmed runtime execution of the substituted artifact.

examplePayloads.label: Locate a download-and-execute call chain lacking signature verification
Substitute an alternate artifact via a test proxy during the download step
examplePayloads.command: # Burp: intercept the update-download response, replace the response body with a benign, clearly-labeled proof-of-concept payload

examplePayloads.label: Confirm execution of the substituted artifact
examplePayloads.command: # observe whether the application executes/loads the substituted payload without any signature-mismatch rejection

variants: No integrity check at all versus a checksum-only check that provides the illusion of protection without any real cryptographic guarantee (an attacker substituting the artifact can also recompute a matching checksum).
Missing verification in an auto-update mechanism versus in a plugin/extension-loading system — both share the same root cause but differ in the specific artifact type and trust context.
mitigation: Cryptographically sign every downloadable artifact with a private key held exclusively by the legitimate publisher, and verify that signature against an embedded, non-user-writable public key before executing/loading the artifact.
Serve downloads exclusively over TLS with certificate pinning, in addition to artifact-level signature verification, as defense in depth.

Ensure the embedded trust anchor (public key/certificate) cannot be overwritten by a lower-privileged process or user, since a locally-tamperable trust anchor undermines even a correctly-implemented signature check.
Treat any download-and-execute code path as a high-priority target during security-focused code review, given its inherent broad reach and typically elevated execution trust.

reference.standard: A08:2021 - Software and Data Integrity Failures
links: CWE-345 (Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity)
CWE-347 (Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature)

items.title: Missing Output Encoding
items.prerequisites: Read access to output-generation source code across multiple contexts (HTML rendering, a generated CSV/report file, a log message, an OS command constructed from application data). A running build of the application to confirm the identified missing-encoding gap at runtime for the specific output context.
items.whatItIs: The application generates output — a CSV file, a shell command, a log entry — without applying the specific escaping rules that particular format actually needs, for data that might contain characters with special meaning there. This is different from the more well-known HTML/script-escaping issue (that's its own separate finding) — this covers other output formats, like a CSV file that Excel might interpret as a formula, or a log entry that could be used to fake or corrupt other log lines.
items.rootCause: Every different output format — HTML, CSV, a shell command, a log line — has its own specific set of characters that need special handling, and its own correct way of escaping them. It's common for a developer to correctly handle the most obvious one (HTML) while overlooking that a less obviously 'output-like' spot — generating a CSV export, writing a log line — needs its own, different, equally necessary escaping that never got added.
items.impact: The output context decides what happens. In a CSV export, a field beginning with an equals sign or similar character is interpreted as a formula when the file is opened in spreadsheet software, running attacker-chosen logic on the victim's machine. In logs, an injected line break can corrupt the log structure or forge entries. And if unescaped output later reaches another interpreter, it becomes an injection flaw there instead.
stepsToIdentify: Identify every distinct output-generation context in the application beyond the primary HTML-rendering path: CSV/spreadsheet exports, log-writing calls, and any place where earlier output becomes later input to another process.
For each context, confirm whether context-appropriate encoding/escaping is applied to any user-controllable data included in that output.

Build and run the application, then populate a test field with a context-specific injection-indicator value (a formula-triggering prefix for CSV, a newline sequence for logs) and generate the corresponding output.
Inspect the resulting output for evidence that the special-meaning character was passed through unescaped rather than neutralized.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes output-generation testing against a running build of the reviewed application for the specific context identified.
Populate a test field with a context-specific injection payload (e.g. `=cmd|' /C calc'!A0` for a CSV-formula-injection test).
Trigger the corresponding output-generation feature (export the CSV, write the log entry).
Confirm the payload is present unescaped in the resulting output, and, for CSV specifically, confirm it would trigger formula execution when opened in common spreadsheet software.
Document the exact source location of the missing context-specific encoding and the confirmed runtime impact.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for CSV/export generation without formula-injection escaping
Test CSV formula-injection via a crafted field value
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/profile -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"displayName":"=cmd|\x27 /C calc\x27!A0"}'
# then trigger the CSV export feature and inspect the resulting file

examplePayloads.label: Test log-injection via a crafted newline sequence

variants: CSV/formula-injection specifically (a distinct, well-known variant of missing output encoding for spreadsheet-consumed exports) versus log-injection (missing encoding for log-format-specific special characters).

Missing output encoding feeding directly into a downstream command/query interpreter, effectively chaining into a command-injection or SQL-injection finding rather than being a standalone output-encoding issue.
mitigation: Apply context-specific output encoding/escaping for every distinct output format the application generates, not just the primary HTML-rendering path — prefix any CSV field beginning with a formula-triggering character with a single quote or otherwise neutralize it, and escape/reject control characters in log output.
Use well-maintained libraries for generating CSV/export files and structured log entries that handle context-appropriate escaping by default, rather than manually constructing the output format.

Treat every output-generation context as requiring its own explicit escaping review during a security-focused code audit, rather than assuming XSS-specific HTML-escaping coverage implies coverage everywhere.
Include context-specific injection test cases (CSV-formula, log-injection) in the standard regression-test suite for any feature generating that output type.

links: CWE-1236 (Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File)
CWE-117 (Improper Output Neutralization for Logs)

items.title: Open Redirect (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to redirect-handling source code (a login-redirect, a logout-redirect, a generic "return to previous page" feature). A running build of the application and a browser or curl to confirm the identified open-redirect at runtime.
items.whatItIs: A feature that redirects the user to a web address supplied in the request — commonly a 'take me back to where I was' redirect after login — does so without checking that the destination is actually somewhere on the same site. This is confirmed by finding the redirect code and seeing the destination gets passed straight through with no check against a list of allowed, internal destinations.
items.rootCause: Just accepting and redirecting to whatever address the request supplies is the simplest way to build a 'return to previous page' feature. Actually checking that the destination is genuinely internal — not some random external site — takes an extra step that's easy to skip since it's not obviously necessary just from a functional standpoint.
items.impact: An attacker builds a link pointing at the application's own trusted domain that silently forwards the victim to a malicious destination. This helps phishing, because the visible link looks legitimate and gets clicked more readily. It also launders the malicious destination through a trusted domain, which is often enough to slip past link-reputation and URL-filtering controls.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every code path implementing a redirect based on a caller-supplied URL parameter.
Confirm whether any validation exists restricting the destination to an internal, expected path/domain, versus accepting any URL value supplied.
Build and run the application, then submit the identified redirect parameter with an external test URL and observe whether the application redirects to it.

Assess whether validation, if present, is genuinely robust (an exact-match internal-path allowlist) versus bypassable (a substring/prefix check defeated by a crafted URL like `https://trusted.com.evil-test.com`).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes open-redirect testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Craft a request to the identified redirect feature with the destination parameter set to a controlled, external test URL.
Confirm the application redirects to the external destination.
Where a bypassable validation check is suspected, craft a URL specifically designed to satisfy the flawed check while still redirecting externally.
Document the exact source location of the missing/bypassable validation and the confirmed runtime open-redirect.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for a redirect built directly from a caller-supplied parameter
Test the redirect with an external test destination
Test a suspected bypassable substring/prefix validation check

variants: No validation at all versus a substring/prefix-based check that's bypassable via a crafted lookalike domain.
Open redirect on a post-login flow specifically (higher phishing value, since it follows an apparently-legitimate authentication step) versus a more general, less trust-laden redirect feature.
mitigation: Restrict redirect destinations to an explicit allowlist of internal, expected paths, using an exact match rather than a substring/prefix check.
Where redirecting to an external URL is genuinely required for some legitimate feature, display an interstitial "you are leaving this site" warning page rather than redirecting silently.
Never accept a full external URL as a redirect destination parameter if the feature's actual, legitimate use case only requires redirecting to internal application paths.
Include an automated test asserting the redirect feature rejects an external test destination in the standard regression-test suite.

links: OWASP WSTG-CLNT-04 (Testing for Client-Side URL Redirect)

items.title: Path Traversal (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to file-access source code (any function reading/writing a file based on a caller-supplied path/filename component). A running build of the application and an HTTP client to confirm the identified traversal gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: Code that reads or writes a file based on a filename or path the caller supplies builds the final file location by directly gluing that value onto a base folder path, without checking for or stripping out sequences like '../' that could let someone escape outside the intended folder. This is confirmed by finding the file-access code and seeing there's no check normalizing or validating the path before the file gets accessed.
items.rootCause: Just gluing a base folder path and a caller-supplied piece together is the simplest way to build a file path. Without an explicit step to check the final result actually stays inside the intended folder (or to strip out '../'-style sequences from the input first), a caller-supplied sequence like that gets interpreted by the file system exactly as an attacker intends — walking the path right outside the folder it was supposed to be limited to.
items.impact: An attacker can read any file the application process has permission to access, exposing configuration files, source code or credentials. Where the operation is a write rather than a read, they can overwrite files instead, and overwriting a critical application file typically opens the way to further compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every file-access function that incorporates a caller-supplied filename/path component, and confirm whether the resulting path is normalized and verified to remain within the intended base directory before the file operation executes.
Build and run the application, then submit a traversal-sequence-crafted value (`../../../../etc/passwd` or an OS-appropriate equivalent) to the identified parameter.
Confirm whether the response reflects content from outside the intended base directory, proving the traversal succeeded.
For a write-capable file-access function, similarly test whether a traversal sequence can direct a write operation outside the intended directory.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes path-traversal testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Submit a traversal-sequence-crafted value to the identified vulnerable parameter.
Confirm the resulting response includes content from a file outside the intended base directory.
Where a write-capable path is also identified, demonstrate a benign, non-destructive proof-of-concept write to a location outside the intended directory.
Document the exact source location of the missing path-validation logic and the confirmed runtime traversal exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for direct path concatenation without normalization/validation
Test path traversal against the identified file-read parameter
Test path traversal against a write-capable file-access parameter

variants: Traversal via a straightforward relative-path sequence versus via an encoded/obfuscated variant (URL-encoded, double-encoded, or null-byte-terminated) designed to bypass a partial/naive filtering attempt.
Path-traversal-vulnerable read operation (information disclosure) versus write operation (potential further compromise via overwriting a critical file) — the latter is materially more severe.
mitigation: Normalize the resulting file path (resolving all `../` and symbolic-link components) and explicitly verify it remains within the intended base directory before performing the file operation, rejecting any request where it doesn't.
Where feasible, avoid accepting a caller-supplied path/filename at all — use an internal, indirect identifier mapped server-side to the actual file location instead.
Apply the operating system's own file-system permissions to further restrict what the application process can access, as defense in depth beyond application-level path validation.
Include path-traversal test cases (including encoded/obfuscated variants) in the standard regression-test suite for every file-access endpoint.

links: OWASP WSTG-ATHZ-01 (Testing Directory Traversal File Include)

items.title: Sensitive Data Logging
items.prerequisites: Read access to logging-call source code across representative endpoints. A running build of the application and access to its log output (or log-aggregation system, with client authorization) to confirm the identified logging gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: Logging statements in the code capture sensitive data — a password from a request, an auth token, a card number, or other personal information — and write it directly into the logs. This is confirmed by finding the logging call and seeing that what gets logged includes those sensitive fields instead of a cleaned-up, filtered version.
items.rootCause: Logging an entire request or response is a convenient way to get maximum detail for debugging. It is easy to forget that what gets logged may include fields that should never reach a log file. The risk is highest when the logging line was added quickly during development or while troubleshooting, then never revisited before going live.
items.impact: Anyone with access to the logs or the log aggregation system can read the sensitive data recorded there. That group is usually larger than the set of people authorised to see the same data in its proper home — a wider engineering and support team, plus any third-party logging vendor. Log retention also frequently outlasts the retention applied to the original data, so it persists longer than intended too.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for logging calls that log a complete request/response object, an error object containing embedded request data, or an explicitly-named sensitive variable.
For each candidate, confirm whether the logged content includes genuinely sensitive fields (password, token, card number, PII) rather than a filtered/redacted subset.
Build and run the application, populate representative sensitive test data through normal use, and inspect the actual log output for the presence of that data in plaintext.
Check whether a third-party log-aggregation service is used, which would extend the population with access beyond the organization's own personnel.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes log-content inspection during normal use of a running build of the reviewed application, populated with representative sensitive test data.
Trigger the code path containing the identified logging statement using representative sensitive test data.
Inspect the resulting log output for the presence of that sensitive data in plaintext.
Document the exact source location of the sensitive logging statement and the specific data type confirmed present in the log output.

Recommend a structured logging framework with field-level redaction/masking applied by default to known-sensitive field names, rather than relying on developers to remember to exclude sensitive fields manually at each call site.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for logging calls capturing complete request/response objects
Trigger the identified logging statement with representative sensitive test data
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/login -d '{"username":"test","password":"TestPassword123!"}'
# then inspect the application's log output for this request

variants: Sensitive data logged unconditionally in production versus only in a debug-level log statement that's supposed to be disabled in production but isn't correctly gated.
Sensitive data logged from first-party application code versus from a third-party library/middleware's own default, verbose logging behavior.
mitigation: Remove logging of complete request/response objects containing sensitive fields; log only the specific, non-sensitive fields genuinely needed for debugging/audit purposes.
Implement a centralized log-sanitization/redaction utility applied consistently across all logging calls, automatically masking known-sensitive field names before they're written.
Add a static-analysis rule flagging any logging call referencing a variable/object likely to contain sensitive data as a mandatory code-review item.
Apply an appropriate, minimized log-retention period and access-control restriction to the log-aggregation system itself, as defense in depth.

reference.standard: A09:2021 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
links: CWE-312 (Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information)

items.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code that fetches a URL server-side based on caller-supplied input (a webhook-registration handler, a file-import-by-URL feature, a link-preview generator). A running build of the application and a listener you control (Burp Collaborator or netcat) to confirm the identified SSRF at runtime.
items.whatItIs: A function that makes a server-side request to a web address built from caller-supplied input does so with no restriction on where that address is allowed to point. This is confirmed by finding the code that makes the outbound request and tracing its target address back to something the caller can actually influence.
items.rootCause: This URL-fetching code was built to support a real, useful feature without adding any restriction on where it's allowed to send requests — treating the caller-supplied address as trustworthy, rather than as untrusted data that could point the server's own network requests anywhere it's able to reach.
items.impact: An attacker makes the server issue requests on their behalf to internal-only resources, or to the cloud provider's metadata service. The server's own network position and trust carry the request somewhere the attacker has no direct route to, which is exactly what makes this more than a curiosity.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every function performing a server-side HTTP(S) request based on caller-supplied input and confirm whether any destination-restriction logic (an allowlist, an internal-IP block) exists before the request is made.
Build and run the application, then submit a request with the target-URL parameter pointing at a listener you control to confirm the server fetches it.
Submit the same request with the target-URL parameter pointing at an internal/link-local address and observe the response for reflected content.
Test whether alternate URL schemes (`file://`, `gopher://`) are also accepted, indicating a broader SSRF primitive.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SSRF testing against a running build of the reviewed application, including probing internal/link-local address ranges.
Submit a test request with the target-URL parameter pointing at a Collaborator/controlled listener to confirm out-of-band request delivery.
Submit a request targeting the cloud metadata service address (or another internal target agreed with the client) and inspect the response for reflected internal content.
Where metadata-service access is confirmed, attempt to retrieve IAM credentials and validate their scope with a minimal, read-only check.
Document the exact source location of the missing destination-restriction logic and the specific internal resource successfully reached.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for an outbound-request call using caller-supplied URL input without destination restriction
Confirm out-of-band request delivery via a controlled listener
Probe the cloud metadata service via the vulnerable parameter

variants: Blind SSRF (confirmable only via out-of-band interaction) versus a variant reflecting fetched content directly in the response, enabling full internal-content disclosure.
Destination-restriction absent entirely versus present but bypassable via a DNS-rebinding attack against a hostname-only allowlist check that doesn't resolve and verify the actual destination IP.
mitigation: Restrict server-side URL-fetching functionality to an explicit allowlist of permitted schemes and destination hosts, rejecting any URL outside that allowlist.
Block requests to internal/link-local/loopback address ranges at the network egress level, as defense in depth beyond application-level allowlisting.
Resolve and verify the supplied URL's hostname to an IP address server-side before fetching, checking that resolved IP against the internal/link-local blocklist to prevent DNS-rebinding bypass.
Use Instance Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2) with a hop-limit restriction where cloud metadata access is genuinely needed by the application itself.

links: OWASP API Security Top 10 - API7:2023 Server Side Request Forgery

items.title: Use of Vulnerable Dependency
items.prerequisites: Read access to the application's dependency manifest (package.json/requirements.txt/pom.xml and their corresponding lock files). A software-composition-analysis (SCA) tool (npm audit, OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, or an equivalent) to scan the manifest for known vulnerabilities.
items.whatItIs: The application depends on a third-party library at a version with one or more known, publicly documented security bugs. This is found by directly scanning the list of dependencies against a database of known vulnerabilities, rather than waiting to see an actual attack happen.
items.rootCause: Dependencies typically get locked to a specific version when they're first added, and only get updated when a new feature is needed or there's a scheduled window to do the testing an update requires. Without a regular, deliberate process to check dependencies against new vulnerability disclosures, a locked-in version just quietly builds up known, unpatched security bugs over time.
items.impact: Any known flaw in the outdated dependency becomes exploitable against the application, provided the application's own use of that library actually reaches the vulnerable code. That range is wide. It may sit in a code path the application never calls, making it low risk, or it may be directly reachable and yield remote code execution or an authentication bypass.
stepsToIdentify: Run a software-composition-analysis scan against the application's dependency manifest/lock file.
Review the resulting CVE findings, prioritizing Critical/High severity issues with a known public exploit.
For each Critical/High finding, review the application's actual usage of the affected library/function to assess whether the vulnerable code path is genuinely reachable.
Cross-reference the dependency's pinned version against its current, actively-maintained release to quantify how far behind the integration has drifted.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes dependency scanning and, where a specific reachable CVE is identified, exploitation testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Run the SCA scan and record the full CVE findings list with severity ratings.
For the highest-severity, most-reachable finding, research whether a public proof-of-concept exists for that specific CVE.

Where safe and clearly scoped, demonstrate the specific vulnerability against a non-production test build to confirm real-world exploitability rather than relying on the scanner's severity rating alone.
Document the specific library, its version drift from current, and the prioritized CVE list with reachability assessment for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Run a dependency vulnerability scan (Node.js example)
Run an equivalent scan for a Java/Maven project
Cross-reference a specific flagged library version against its current release

variants: Vulnerable dependency present but its vulnerable code path not actually reachable by the application's specific usage pattern (lower practical risk) versus one actively invoked in the application's core functionality.
Vulnerability introduced via a direct dependency versus a transitive (indirect) dependency, requiring dependency-tree-level scanning rather than only checking directly-declared libraries.
mitigation: Establish a recurring dependency-audit process (ideally automated via CI/CD-integrated SCA scanning) to catch newly-disclosed CVEs against dependencies promptly.
Update outdated dependencies to their current, patched versions on a regular cadence, budgeting for associated regression-testing effort as routine maintenance.
Where a specific dependency has a poor security-maintenance track record, evaluate replacing it with a better-maintained alternative.
Maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) for the application's dependencies to make future vulnerability cross-referencing faster and more reliable.

links: CVE/NVD (nvd.nist.gov) for specific dependency CVE lookups

items.title: XML External Entity (Source-Identified)
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code that parses XML input (an API endpoint accepting XML, a file-import feature processing an uploaded XML/SVG/DOCX-family document). A running build of the application and an HTTP client to confirm the identified XXE gap at runtime.
items.whatItIs: The application processes XML data supplied by a caller using a parser that hasn't turned off a feature called external entity resolution. This is confirmed directly by finding the XML-parsing code and checking whether the specific settings that disable this risky feature are actually turned on — or left at their default, permissive state.
items.rootCause: Most XML parsing tools have historically allowed this feature by default, for compatibility with the XML standard. Unless the application specifically turns it off when setting up the parser, any XML it processes — including XML from an untrusted source — can reference external content that the parser will go fetch, whether that's reading a local file or making an outbound network request the attacker directed.
items.impact: An attacker supplies XML containing a malicious external reference. On parsing, that reads and returns the contents of a local file, such as a system file or an application configuration file holding credentials. The same technique can instead trigger an outbound request to an internal address or the cloud metadata service. And with some parser configurations it causes a denial of service, where a small file expands into gigabytes of memory.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every XML-parsing call site handling caller-supplied input, and confirm the parser's configuration explicitly disables DOCTYPE declarations, external entity resolution, and external DTD loading.
Where the parser configuration is default/unconfigured for these settings, treat this as a strong indicator of vulnerability pending runtime confirmation.
Build and run the application, then submit a crafted XML payload containing an external entity referencing a benign, verifiable local file or an out-of-band listener.
Confirm whether the response reflects the referenced file's content, or whether an out-of-band request is received, proving the entity was resolved.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes XXE testing against a running build of the reviewed application's XML-parsing endpoint.
Craft an XML payload defining an external entity referencing a benign, verifiable local file or a controlled out-of-band listener.
Submit the payload to the identified endpoint and confirm entity resolution via reflected content or an out-of-band callback.
Where confirmed, test for the SSRF-via-XXE variant by referencing an internal/cloud-metadata URL in the entity definition.
Document the exact source location of the permissive parser configuration and the confirmed runtime XXE exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Search source for XML parser instantiation without external-entity-disabling configuration
Craft an XXE payload to read a benign local test file
examplePayloads.command: curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/api/import -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">]><data>&xxe;</data>'

examplePayloads.label: Craft an out-of-band XXE confirmation payload
examplePayloads.command: curl -s -X POST https://app.target.com/api/import -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://<your-collaborator-id>.oastify.com/xxe-confirmed">]><data>&xxe;</data>'

variants: Classic file-read XXE via a `file://` entity versus SSRF-via-XXE via an entity referencing an internal/cloud-metadata URL.

XXE reachable via a directly-accepted XML endpoint versus via a file-format that embeds XML internally (SVG, DOCX/XLSX's underlying XML structure, a SOAP request body) that isn't obviously an "XML endpoint" on its surface.
mitigation: Explicitly disable DOCTYPE declarations, external general entities, external parameter entities, and external DTD loading in every XML parser configuration used by the application, following the specific library's documented hardening guidance.
Where possible, use a data format that doesn't support external entities at all (JSON) instead of XML for any new API design.
Apply the same hardened parser configuration to any file format with an embedded XML structure (SVG uploads, Office Open XML documents), not just endpoints explicitly documented as "XML APIs."
Include an automated test submitting a benign XXE-probe payload against every XML-accepting endpoint in the CI pipeline, asserting the entity is not resolved.

links: OWASP WSTG-INPV-07 (Testing for XML Injection)

items.title: CI/CD Workflow Injection and Untrusted Pipeline Triggers
items.prerequisites: Read access to the repository's pipeline definitions: workflow files, pipeline YAML, or build configuration. Understanding of which events trigger each pipeline and which of those events can be caused by someone outside the organisation.
