Authorisation to review pipeline configuration and, where agreed, to open a test pull request against a designated branch.
items.whatItIs: Pipeline definitions interpolate context values — branch names, pull request titles, commit messages, issue bodies — directly into shell steps. Those values are attacker-controlled on any pipeline that runs for external contributions. The interpolation happens before the shell sees the line, so quoting inside the script does not help: the substituted text becomes part of the command. Triggers that run with repository secrets against untrusted code make this immediately serious.
items.rootCause: Template interpolation is the documented way to use context values, and the distinction between trusted and untrusted context is not visible in the syntax. Triggers that run in the base repository's context with access to secrets exist so that pipelines can comment on pull requests, and that convenience is what makes them dangerous. Pipelines are also frequently exempt from the code review that protects application code.
items.impact: Command execution on the build runner with whatever the pipeline holds: repository secrets, registry push credentials, cloud deployment roles, signing keys. That is a supply chain compromise rather than a build server incident, because those credentials publish artefacts that downstream consumers trust. The attacker frequently needs no repository access at all, only the ability to open a pull request or file an issue.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all pipeline definitions and record which events trigger each one.
Identify triggers that run for external contributions, particularly those executing in the base repository's context.
Search step scripts for interpolated context values, separating trusted metadata from attacker-controllable fields.
Determine which secrets each pipeline can access and what those secrets permit.
Check whether third-party actions are pinned to a commit digest or referenced by a mutable tag.
Establish whether pipeline changes require review, and whether self-hosted runners are shared across repositories.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers opening a test pull request or issue against a designated repository.
Identify a pipeline that runs on an externally triggerable event and interpolates a controllable field.
Construct a benign payload in that field that produces observable output rather than exfiltrating anything.
Trigger the pipeline and confirm from the build log that the payload executed as a command.
Enumerate which secrets are present in the environment without printing their values.
Stop at proof of execution and report the trigger, the field and the reachable secrets as one finding.

Find interpolated context
Vulnerable pattern

examplePayloads.label: Action pinning check

variants: A pipeline that checks out the pull request's code and runs its build scripts while holding base repository secrets.
A third-party action referenced by a mutable tag, which its maintainer or an attacker can repoint.
A self-hosted runner shared between repositories, where one repository's compromise reaches the others.
Injection through a branch name rather than a title, which is controllable on any fork.
mitigation: Pass context values through environment variables and reference them as shell variables, rather than interpolating them into the script text.
Avoid triggers that combine untrusted code with secret access; where one is required, run untrusted code in a separate job with no secrets.
Pin third-party actions to a full commit digest rather than a tag.
Grant each pipeline the minimum token permissions it needs, defaulting to read-only.
Require review for pipeline definition changes to the same standard as application code.
Prefer ephemeral runners, and never share a self-hosted runner between repositories with different trust levels.

items.title: Dependency Confusion and Lockfile Integrity Gaps
items.prerequisites: Read access to the repository's dependency manifests, lockfiles and package manager configuration. Knowledge of which internal registries the organisation operates and which package names are internal. Authorisation to review configuration and, where a demonstration is agreed, to reserve a name on a public registry without publishing functional code.
items.whatItIs: Internal package names are not reserved on public registries, and most package managers resolve a name across all configured sources, preferring the highest version. So an attacker who publishes an internal-sounding name publicly at a high version number can have it installed in place of the internal package. Lockfiles mitigate this only when they are committed, complete, and installed with a command that honours them rather than resolving afresh.
items.rootCause: Package managers were designed for a single public namespace, and multi-source resolution was added without a mechanism to bind a name to a source. Version preference beats source preference in most resolvers by default. Scoping and namespacing solve it but require deliberate configuration. Install commands that re-resolve instead of honouring the lockfile are common in CI, where the difference between install and clean-install is not obvious.
items.impact: A malicious package executes at install time, frequently with the privileges of the build process, which puts it inside CI with access to source and secrets. Because installation is a routine step, it is neither reviewed nor alerted on. Where the compromised build produces published artefacts, the effect propagates to everything downstream. Internal package names are also often discoverable from published artefacts, error messages or job postings.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate internal package names referenced in manifests and determine whether each is scoped or namespaced.
Check whether any internal name is unregistered on the corresponding public registry.
Review the package manager configuration for how multiple sources are resolved and whether internal names are pinned to a source.
Verify that lockfiles are committed and cover every dependency including transitive ones.
Check which install command the pipeline uses, and whether it honours the lockfile or re-resolves.
Establish whether install-time scripts are permitted, since that is the execution path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, and agree that any public name reservation contains no functional code and is removed afterwards.
List internal package names and check public registry availability for each.
Where a name is available, reserve it with a placeholder package at a version above the internal one.
In a controlled build environment, run the project's install command and record which source the package resolved from.
Confirm whether the lockfile prevented the substitution, since that distinguishes an exposure from an exploitable path.
Remove the reserved package and report which names remain unprotected.

Public availability check

Correct scoping
Lockfile honouring check

variants: A public mirror or proxy that falls through to the public registry when an internal name is not found.
Typosquatting a popular public dependency rather than shadowing an internal name.
A transitive dependency introducing the confusion, so the manifest under review looks clean.
Container base images resolved by mutable tag, which is the same substitution problem at the image layer.
mitigation: Scope or namespace all internal packages and bind that scope to the internal registry in configuration.
Reserve internal package names defensively on the relevant public registries.
Use a single internal registry that proxies the public one, rather than configuring multiple sources in the client.
Commit complete lockfiles and use install commands that honour them exactly, failing when the lockfile is out of date.
Disable install-time scripts by default and allowlist the few packages that genuinely require them.
Verify integrity hashes on install and fail the build when a package does not match its recorded hash.

items.title: Secrets Exposed in Version Control History
items.prerequisites: Clone access to the repository, including full history rather than a shallow clone. Where the repository is public, no access is required at all. Authorisation to scan history and to handle any credentials recovered, with an agreed procedure since the values are frequently live.
items.whatItIs: A secret removed in a later commit remains in every earlier commit, and cloning retrieves all of them. Deleting the file changes only the current tree. The same applies to secrets in commit messages, in branches never merged, and in objects left unreferenced after a rewrite, which remain retrievable until garbage collection runs. A review of the current working tree therefore says nothing about what the repository discloses.
items.rootCause: Rewriting history is disruptive and requires coordination across everyone with a clone, so the usual response to a committed secret is a follow-up commit removing it. That feels like remediation and is not. Scanning tools are frequently run against the working tree rather than across history. Rotation is also skipped because the secret appears to be gone, leaving a live credential in a place anyone with clone access can read.
items.impact: A live credential in history is exposed to everyone who can clone the repository, which for a public repository means everyone. Cloud keys, database credentials and signing keys are all commonly found this way, and automated scanners find them within minutes of a public push. Because the credential is usually still valid, the finding is immediately actionable by an attacker while looking resolved to the organisation.
stepsToIdentify: Clone the full history rather than a shallow copy, and include all branches and tags.
Scan every commit with a secret detection tool rather than scanning the working tree.
Search commit messages separately, since they are not covered by tree-based scans.
Check for unreferenced objects from previous rewrites, which remain retrievable until pruned.
For each candidate, determine whether it is live by structure and expiry rather than by authenticating.
Establish whether the repository was ever public, and for how long, since that determines the exposure window.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers history scanning and agree in advance how recovered credentials will be handled.
Clone with full history and fetch all references.
Run detection across the complete history and collect candidates with their commit and file location.
Filter out test and placeholder values, which dominate raw results.
For genuine candidates, assess validity from structure and metadata, and only test authentication where explicitly authorised.
Report each finding with the commit, the date it was introduced and the exposure window, since those drive the rotation decision.

variants: A secret in a branch that was never merged and is therefore absent from the main history view.
A repository that was public for a period before being made private, where clones already exist externally.
A secret in a Git submodule or in an LFS object, which tree-based scanning misses.
Credentials in CI configuration history, which is frequently less reviewed than application code.
mitigation: Rotate every credential found in history and treat it as disclosed, regardless of whether the file was later removed.
Scan the full history in CI rather than only the working tree, and fail the build on detection.
Install pre-commit secret scanning so credentials are caught before they enter history at all.
Rewrite history to purge confirmed secrets, and coordinate the force-push with everyone holding a clone.
Move all secrets to a secret store referenced at runtime, so there is nothing to commit.
Treat any period of public exposure as full disclosure, since automated scanners find public secrets within minutes.

items.title: Prototype Pollution in JavaScript Object Handling
items.prerequisites: A JavaScript or TypeScript codebase performing recursive merges, deep clones, or object construction from user-supplied data. Read access to the source, including dependencies where the vulnerable merge frequently lives. Ability to run the application or its tests to confirm behaviour, since the impact depends on what reads the polluted property.
items.whatItIs: Assigning to a key named __proto__ or constructor.prototype on a normal object modifies the prototype that every other object inherits from. A recursive merge that copies keys from user input without excluding those names therefore lets an attacker add a property to every object in the process. The vulnerability is in the merge; the impact comes later, wherever code reads a property it expects to be absent.
items.rootCause: Property assignment in JavaScript treats these keys as ordinary strings, so a naive merge walks into them without any special handling. Recursive merge, deep clone and query-string parsing helpers are written generically and frequently omit the check. Because the effect appears in unrelated code much later, it does not look like a data-flow problem in review, and the merge itself reads as correct.
items.impact: Effects range from denial of service to remote code execution depending on what consumes the polluted property. A common escalation is polluting a property that a template engine, a command-spawning helper or an option-defaulting routine reads, turning the pollution into execution. Authorisation bypass is also common where code checks for a property whose absence means denied, since pollution makes it present on every object.
stepsToIdentify: Locate recursive merge, deep clone, deep set and object-from-path functions in application code and dependencies.
Determine whether each excludes __proto__, constructor and prototype before assigning.
Identify which of them receive user-controlled input, including query strings, JSON bodies and configuration files.
Trace where the application reads properties with a default fallback, since those are the consumption points.
Look for gadget candidates: template options, child process options, and library configuration read from object properties.
Check whether objects that hold user data are created with a null prototype, which removes the inheritance path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers sending crafted payloads to the application.
Identify an input reaching a merge function and send a payload assigning a benign marker property.
Confirm pollution by observing that an unrelated, newly created object exposes the marker.
Map the consumption points and find one whose behaviour changes when the marker property exists.
Demonstrate the most severe reachable consequence, choosing an observable effect over a destructive one.
Report the merge site and the gadget together, since the merge alone is the vulnerability but the gadget determines severity.

examplePayloads.label: Find merge implementations
Missing key guard
examplePayloads.command: grep -rn 'for (const key in source)' -A4 src/ | grep -L '__proto__'

examplePayloads.label: JSON body payload
Constructor path payload
Query string payload
Confirm pollution
examplePayloads.command: node -e 'const o={}; console.log(({}).polluted)'   # after triggering, a fresh object exposes the property

variants: Pollution via a query string parser that builds nested objects from bracket notation.
Client-side pollution leading to cross-site scripting through a library that reads options from object properties.
Pollution through a configuration or environment file parsed into an object.
A vulnerable transitive dependency, where the application's own merge code is correct.
mitigation: Reject or skip the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype in every recursive merge, clone and deep-set function.
Create objects that hold user-supplied data with a null prototype, so there is no inheritance path to pollute.
Freeze Object.prototype at application startup where the runtime and dependencies permit it.
Validate request bodies against a schema that rejects unexpected keys rather than merging them.
Prefer Map over plain objects for user-controlled key-value data.
Keep dependencies current and scan for known prototype pollution advisories, since the vulnerable merge is often not your own code.

items.title: Disabled TLS Certificate Validation in Source
items.prerequisites: Read access to source code making outbound network calls, including server-to-server integrations and internal service communication. Knowledge of which HTTP clients and TLS libraries the codebase uses. Ability to search across the repository and its configuration, since the setting is frequently applied in configuration rather than in code.
items.whatItIs: Certificate validation gets disabled during development to work around a self-signed certificate in a test environment, and the change frequently ships. The forms it takes are varied — a verify flag set to false, a trust manager that accepts everything, a hostname verifier that always returns true, an environment variable that disables verification globally — so a search for one pattern misses the others. The connection remains encrypted, which is why nothing appears broken.
items.rootCause: The failure it produces in development is immediate and obstructive, and the workaround is one line, so it is applied under time pressure and forgotten. Because the symptom disappears and the connection still uses TLS, there is no later signal that the control is off. Some HTTP client libraries also make disabling verification easier than configuring a custom trust store, which points developers at the worse option.
items.impact: TLS without certificate validation provides encryption but no authentication, so any adversary positioned on the path can present their own certificate and read or modify the traffic. For a server-to-server integration carrying credentials or financial instructions, that is complete compromise of the channel. The failure is silent in every direction: no error, no log entry, and no difference visible to monitoring.
stepsToIdentify: Search the codebase for verification flags across every HTTP client and TLS library in use.
Look for custom trust managers and hostname verifiers that accept all inputs.
Check configuration files and environment variables for global verification switches.
Determine whether the setting is conditional on environment, and whether the condition is reliable in production.
Review certificate pinning implementations, since a broken pin is sometimes resolved by disabling validation.
Confirm behaviour at runtime by presenting an untrusted certificate and observing whether the client proceeds.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers intercepting the application's outbound connections in a test environment.
Identify each outbound integration and the client library it uses.
Position an intercepting proxy with a certificate not present in any trust store the application uses.
Trigger each integration and record which connections proceed despite the untrusted certificate.
For any that proceed, confirm the traffic is readable and note what it carries.
Report per integration, since validation is usually disabled on specific clients rather than globally.

mitigation: Never disable certificate validation; install the internal CA into the trust store instead.
Add a static analysis rule that fails the build on any verification-disabling pattern, covering every client library in use.
Ban environment-level verification switches in deployment configuration and container images.
Verify the hostname as well as the certificate chain, since skipping the hostname check accepts any valid certificate.
Use properly issued certificates in development and test environments, removing the reason the workaround is reached for.
Test outbound connections against an untrusted certificate as part of release testing, since the failure is otherwise silent.

items.title: Missing Tenant Predicate in Multi-Tenant Query Construction
items.prerequisites: Read access to the source of a multi-tenant application where tenant separation is enforced in query construction rather than at the database level. Understanding of how tenant context is established and propagated. Two tenant accounts for runtime confirmation, and authorisation to attempt cross-tenant access.
items.whatItIs: Where tenants share a database, separation depends on every query carrying a predicate restricting results to the caller's tenant. That predicate is added by the developer on each query, so it is omitted the way any repeated manual step is omitted: on a new query, on a reporting endpoint written in a hurry, on a raw query written to bypass the ORM for performance. One missing predicate exposes every tenant's rows through an otherwise ordinary endpoint.
items.rootCause: The predicate is a convention rather than an enforced property, and nothing fails when it is absent — the query returns more rows, which looks like working code. Aggregate and reporting queries are particularly affected because they are written against the whole table by nature. Raw SQL written to optimise a slow path escapes whatever ORM-level scoping exists, and background jobs frequently run without any tenant context at all.
items.impact: Complete cross-tenant data disclosure through a legitimate, authenticated endpoint. For a SaaS platform this is the most serious failure available, since the separation between customers is the product's fundamental promise. Detection is unlikely because every request is authenticated and authorised at the user level, and the additional rows returned look like ordinary result sets in any log.
stepsToIdentify: Establish how tenant context is derived and whether it comes from a verified claim or from a request parameter.
Enumerate every query construction site, including ORM calls, raw SQL, stored procedures and reporting queries.
Determine whether the tenant predicate is applied automatically by a base repository or added manually per query.
Search for raw queries and aggregate queries specifically, since those most often bypass any automatic scoping.
Review background jobs and scheduled tasks, which frequently run without a tenant context.
Check whether the database enforces separation independently, through row-level security or per-tenant credentials.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers cross-tenant access attempts using two accounts you control.
Seed distinctive marker records in the second tenant so cross-tenant leakage is unambiguous.
From the first tenant, exercise every endpoint and inspect responses for the markers.
Concentrate on reporting, aggregate, search and export endpoints, which are the usual sites.
Where a count or total is returned rather than rows, compare it against the first tenant's own data to detect inflation.
Report each affected endpoint individually, since the fix is per query unless the architecture is changed.

variants: Tenant identifier taken from a request header or parameter rather than from a verified token claim.
A background job or scheduled report running without tenant context and emailing results to the wrong tenant.
A cache keyed without the tenant identifier, serving one tenant's cached response to another.
A search index containing all tenants' documents with filtering applied only in the query the application happens to send.
mitigation: Enforce separation at the database using row-level security or per-tenant credentials, so a missing predicate fails closed.
Derive tenant context from a verified token claim and never from a client-supplied parameter.
Apply the tenant predicate in a base repository or query interceptor rather than relying on it being added per query.
Require review and justification for any raw query that bypasses the scoped data access layer.
Include the tenant identifier in every cache key and search index filter.
Test cross-tenant isolation with seeded marker data as a standing part of release testing, since one new query reintroduces the risk.
